docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_document::set
docs.text:
// (1)
template<typename V>
view_type set(view_type target, V&& value);

// (2)
template<typename V>
view_type set(view_type object, string_view_t key, V&& value);

// (3)
template<typename I, typename V>
view_type set(view_type array, I idx, V&& value);

// (4)
template<typename V>
view_type set(const json_pointer& ptr, V&& value);

Only an editable document (view_mode::editable, e.g. json_editable_document) has set; calling it on a read-only basic_json_document fails to compile (static_assert).

  1. Replaces the value target refers to with value.
  2. Sets the member key of the object object to value: assigns it if object already has a member with this key — the first one, should the key occur more than once, and the later duplicates are then dropped (see the Notes below) — or appends a new member at the end otherwise. A null object first becomes an empty object.
  3. Assigns value to the element at index idx of the array array, which must already exist (idx < array.size()).
  4. Sets the value the JSON pointer ptr refers to, relative to root(), to value. The parent of the target must already exist: an object member is set as in 2. (added if it does not exist yet), an array element is assigned as in 3., and a last reference token of "-", or equal to the size of the array, appends value instead, exactly as push_back would. A null parent becomes what basic_json::operator[] with a JSON pointer makes of it: an array if the last reference token is "-" or consists of digits only (for an index beyond 0, the array is first filled with null values up to that index), an object otherwise. An empty ptr sets root() itself, as in 1.

In every overload, value is accepted three ways: a basic_json_view of any document — read-only or editable, and it does not have to be target's/object's/array's own document — which is copied so that nothing is shared with the source document afterward; a BasicJsonType value; or anything BasicJsonType can be constructed from (numbers, strings, bool, nullptr, containers, ...).

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: V the type of value, deduced; see above for what is accepted. I an integral type other than bool, deduced (overloads taking a bool or a non-integral type for idx do not participate in overload resolution).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: target (in) the value to replace object (in) the object (or null value) whose member to set array (in) the array whose element to assign key (in) the key of the member to set idx (in) the index of the element to assign; a negative value throws (see Exceptions) ptr (in) a JSON pointer to the value to set, relative to root() value (in) the new value

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
1. a view of target, now holding value
  2. a view of the member key of object, now holding value
  3. a view of the element idx of array, now holding value
  4. a view of the value ptr refers to, now holding value

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Basic exception safety: value is fully encoded — including the checks below — into storage owned by the document before anything already reachable from root() is touched, so a failure while encoding value (an invalid argument, or std::bad_alloc) leaves the document completely unchanged, other than memory allocated for the encoding that is not reclaimed. A failure of a later allocation — while an edited array or object switches from its parsed layout to a growable block, see Notes — can still leave a partial effect, such as a null object/array argument already turned into an empty object/array even though value itself was not linked in. Likewise, a failure of value in 4. leaves a null parent that is set with an index beyond 0 already filled with the null values before the index.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
1. Throws type_error.302 if value is a discarded view, or a discarded BasicJsonType value (e.g. BasicJsonType(value_t::discarded)) — an object or array value, of either kind, is fine and is encoded as a whole subtree.
  2. Throws type_error.305 if object is neither an object nor null — the same message operator[] throws for a string argument on such a value. Throws type_error.316 if key is not valid UTF-8, with the same message BasicJsonType::dump() gives for that string. Also throws what 1. throws for value.
  3. Throws type_error.305 if array is not an array — the same message operator[] throws for a numeric argument on such a value. Throws out_of_range.401 if idx is negative, or if idx >= array.size(). Also throws what 1. throws for value.
  4. Throws what at throws (overload 3) for resolving ptr's parent, except that a missing object member or an array index equal to the array's size at the very last reference token is not an error there (it becomes a new member or an appended element) instead of out_of_range.403/out_of_range.402. For the last reference token itself: if the parent is an object (or a primitive value, where it throws type_error.305), throws what 2. throws; if the parent is an array, throws what 3. throws for an index that is out of range, or, for a token that is not a valid array index, parse_error.106 (a leading '0'), parse_error.109 (not a number), out_of_range.410 (too large for size_type), or out_of_range.404 (an empty token); the same errors are thrown for a null parent and a token of digits (the parent is not changed then), and out_of_range.401 if the index is 4294967295 or more. Also throws what 1. throws for value.

Every overload also throws type_error.319 if value is (or contains) a binary value — BasicJsonType can hold one, but a json_document cannot — and invalid_iterator.202 ("view does not belong to this document") if target/object/array is a discarded view or a view of a different document (overloads 1-3 only; overload 4 always starts from this document's own root()).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
1. Linear in the size of value (encoding it into the document's storage): constant for a scalar, linear in the number of nested values for an array or object. If target is itself an array or object that spans more than one node in its parent's original, unedited layout, and value is a scalar, replacing it additionally costs time linear in the size of the document, the first time (the parent of target is looked up from root(), and then switches to links) — see Notes. Once the parent has links, target is replaced in constant time: setting every element of a large array one after the other is linear overall. To avoid the lookup altogether, use 3. (or 2. for an object), which know the parent.
  2. Linear in the number of members of object, to find an existing member with key, plus the complexity of 1. for value.
  3. Constant, plus the complexity of 1. for value.
  4. Linear in the number of reference tokens of ptr and, for each token, in the number of members of the object at that level or the index into the array (as at), plus the complexity of 2. or 3. for the last token; for a null parent and an index, linear in the index.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Duplicate keys

If object already has more than one member with key (2.), the first one is assigned value and every later member with the same key is removed — so that a lookup, an iteration, and materialize() of object afterward all agree on a single value for key, the same way operator[] already picks the first occurrence of a duplicate key for reading. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[].

Setting a member (2.) or an element (3., through 4.) of an array or object whose elements have not been edited before switches it from its parsed layout to a growable block holding links to its elements; a later push_back or set on the same container reuses that block, growing it (amortized constant time) only once it runs out of room. This never moves an element itself — only where the container's links to its elements live — so a view of an element stays valid, but any iterator already taken over the container is invalidated, since it was walking the old layout. See Edits for what stays valid across an edit in general.

The same switch happens, for the same reason, when overload 1. replaces a multi-node array/object value with a scalar: the parent's element sequence is what has to switch to links, not target itself, because the parent originally stepped over target's whole subtree by its node count, which no longer applies once target is a one-node scalar.

  • insert - insert an element into an array
  • erase - remove an object member, an array element, or the value a JSON pointer refers to
  • root - the view of the root value, the starting point of overload 4

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_document::shrink_to_fit
docs.text:
void shrink_to_fit();

Releases capacity that is no longer needed, both of the node index and of the buffer for decoded strings (strings that contained escape sequences), e.g. after read() replaced a large document with a much smaller one. Like std::vector::shrink_to_fit(), this is a non-binding request: the library may keep more capacity than strictly necessary.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: if an exception is thrown, there are no changes to the document.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc if the reallocation fails; on exception, the document is unchanged.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in node_count() plus the length of the decoded strings.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The node index of a small document (an estimate of up to 1024 nodes, which is up to about 4 KiB of minified text) is allocated together with the document's header, so that parsing needs one allocation. That part cannot be released separately: shrink_to_fit() only trims a node index that has its own allocation, and the decoded strings.

Invalidates views

Unlike moving the document, shrink_to_fit() invalidates every view taken from this document before the call, including a previously obtained root(): the node index is moved into a new, smaller allocation, and the old one is freed. Take a fresh view from root() after calling this function.

This is unlike std::vector::shrink_to_fit(), which promises nothing about validity but in practice often leaves iterators alone when it did not need to reallocate; here, an implementation that avoids a reallocation when possible would be an internal optimization only, not a guarantee to rely on.

See also

  • memory_usage - the number of bytes held by the document
  • root - the view of the root value
  • Zero-copy JSON views - what releasing memory invalidates

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view
docs.text:
Defined in header <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

template<typename BasicJsonType, view_mode Mode = view_mode::read_only>
class basic_json_view;

A read-only handle to one value of a basic_json_document: two pointers (a pointer to the document and a pointer into its index), trivially copyable. A view is valid as long as

  • the document is alive,
  • the document has not been re-parsed with read() (or parse() into it) or shrunk with shrink_to_fit() since the view was taken, and
  • if the document borrows its source text, that text is still alive and unmodified (floating-point values and unescaped strings are read from it lazily).

Moving the document itself does not invalidate its views: the index is heap-allocated independently of the basic_json_document object.

basic_json_view provides the read-only part of the BasicJsonType interface:

  • the type-inspection functions
  • element access
  • lookup
  • iteration
  • conversion: get<T>(), get_string(), number_token(), and materialize() to build the BasicJsonType value of a subtree on demand
  • comparison: operator== and operator!= compare two views, or a view and a BasicJsonType value, without ever building a BasicJsonType value for a view; no ordering comparison (operator<) is provided

operator[], at, contains, and value also accept a json_pointer. Unlike basic_json, there are no implicit conversion operators (no operator ValueType()), and no get_ptr() or get_ref(); see get.

basic_json_view itself is always read-only — it never has a set or push_back of its own. A view of an editable document (view_mode::editable) sees every edit made through basic_json_document::set and basic_json_document::push_back: once a value is changed, every view that still refers to it — including ones taken before the change — reads the new value. See Edits.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: BasicJsonType a specialization of basic_json, matching the basic_json_document the view was taken from. Mode a view_mode: whether the view is of an editable document, matching the basic_json_document it was taken from (optional, view_mode::read_only by default). See Edits.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::at
docs.text:
// (1)
basic_json_view at(string_view_t key) const;
basic_json_view at(const char* key) const;
basic_json_view at(const string_t& key) const;

// (2)
basic_json_view at(size_type idx) const;
template<typename IntegerType>
basic_json_view at(IntegerType idx) const;

// (3)
basic_json_view at(const json_pointer& ptr) const;
  1. Returns the value of the object member with key key — the first one, should the key occur more than once (see Notes on duplicate keys).
  2. Returns the array element at index idx. The template accepts every integer type except bool and std::size_t and forwards to the size_type overload, as for operator[]; a negative idx is out of range.
  3. Returns the value a JSON pointer ptr refers to, starting at this value.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: key (in) object key of the element to access idx (in) index of the element to access ptr (in) JSON pointer to the element to access

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
1. the value of the first member with key key
  2. the element at index idx
  3. the value ptr resolves to, starting at this value

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
1. The function can throw the following exceptions, both with the same message as the corresponding call to BasicJsonType::at:
    • Throws type_error.304 if the value is not an object.
    • Throws out_of_range.403 if no member has key key.
  2. The function can throw the following exceptions, both with the same message as the corresponding call to BasicJsonType::at:
    • Throws type_error.304 if the value is not an array.
    • Throws out_of_range.401 if idx >= size().
  3. The function can throw the following exceptions, all with the same message as the corresponding call to BasicJsonType::at:
    • Throws parse_error.106 if an array index in ptr begins with '0'.
    • Throws parse_error.109 if an array index in ptr is not a number.
    • Throws out_of_range.401 if an array index in ptr is out of range.
    • Throws out_of_range.402 if a reference token is "-" at an array — at never inserts an element, so "-" is always invalid.
    • Throws out_of_range.403 if a reference token names an object member that does not exist.
    • Throws out_of_range.404 if ptr cannot be resolved because a reference token is used on a primitive value.

None of these exceptions carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
1. Linear in the number of members: as for ordered_json, members are compared one after another, in document order, stopping at the first match. Each comparison first checks the key's length — already known from the index, without reading the key bytes — before comparing its content. Objects with 128 or more members get a hash index of their keys while parsing, so that a lookup in them takes constant time on average.
  2. Linear in idx: elements are skipped one at a time from the first one, since they are not a fixed size in the index (unlike BasicJsonType's array, which is random-access). Constant if no element of the array is an array or object, since the elements are then adjacent in the index.
  3. Linear in the number of reference tokens of ptr and, for each token, in the number of members of the object at that level (as 1.) or the index into the array (as 2.).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Duplicate keys: the first member wins

If the source text repeats a key, this resolves to the first member with it, not to the last one that materialize() and parse() keep. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[] and Duplicate keys for the reasons and for how to get the last value.

Unlike operator[], which returns a discarded view for a missing key or an out-of-range index, at always throws — exactly as BasicJsonType::at does, and with the same messages, so existing error handling written against BasicJsonType::at keeps working unchanged when switched to a view. This also holds for overload 3: unlike operator[] with a JSON pointer, which returns a discarded view for a missing key or an out-of-range index, at throws for those too (out_of_range.403/out_of_range.401).

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• operator[] - access specified element (returns a discarded view instead of throwing)
  • front, back - access the first or last element
  • BasicJsonType::at - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • json_pointer - JSON pointer type used by overload 3

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::back
docs.text:
basic_json_view back() const;

Returns the last element of an array, the last member value of an object, or the value itself if it is primitive (as for BasicJsonType::back(), a primitive value is a range of one element).

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: The last element or member value. For a primitive value (number, string, boolean), the value itself.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Throws invalid_iterator.214 if the view is null or discarded, or if it is an empty array or object.

This exception does not carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the size of the array or object: unlike front(), which only ever looks at the first element, back() has to walk every element to find where they end, since elements are not a fixed size in the index. Constant if no element of the array is an array or object, since the elements are then adjacent in the index.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Unlike BasicJsonType::back(), which has undefined behavior for an empty array or object, back() throws invalid_iterator.214 for an empty array, an empty object, a null value, or a discarded view.

docs.title: Examples
See also

  • BasicJsonType::back - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::basic_json_view
docs.text:
// (1)
basic_json_view() noexcept = default;

// (2) only for Mode == view_mode::editable
basic_json_view(const basic_json_view<BasicJsonType, view_mode::read_only>& other) noexcept;
  1. Creates an invalid (discarded) view: type() is value_t::discarded and is_discarded() is true.
  2. Converts a view of a read-only document into a view of an editable document (implicitly), so that a function taking a json_editable_view accepts both. The result is a view of the same value of the same read-only document. See view_mode for why there is no conversion the other way.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
other (in) a view of a read-only document with the same BasicJsonType

Apart from these, a view is obtained from a basic_json_document, via root() or by navigating into a container with operator[], at, front, back, find, or iteration.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: these constructors never throw exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::begin
docs.text:
iterator begin() const noexcept;

Returns an iterator to the first element of an array, or the first member value of an object, in document order — the order the values appear in the source text, not sorted by key. A primitive value iterates as a range of one element (itself), and a null value or a discarded view iterates as an empty range.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: Iterator to the first element.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
For an object, iteration visits every member, including all occurrences of a duplicate key — unlike operator[], at, find, and contains, which all resolve to the first member with a given key. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[].

Because objects are iterated in document order rather than sorted by key, the order seen here can differ from what iterating the materialize()d BasicJsonType value would produce: a basic_json object (std::map-backed by default) sorts its keys, while a view does not.

An ordered_json value also keeps document order, but it keeps only one entry per key: as parse() does, it keeps the last value, at the position of the key's first occurrence. The view, in contrast, visits every member, including the duplicates.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::contains
docs.text:
// (1)
bool contains(string_view_t key) const;
bool contains(const char* key) const;
bool contains(const string_t& key) const;

// (2)
bool contains(const json_pointer& ptr) const;
  1. Checks whether the value is an object with a member with key key.
  2. Checks whether a JSON pointer ptr can be resolved, starting at this value.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: key (in) key value to check its existence ptr (in) JSON pointer to check its existence

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
1. true if the value is an object and has a member with key key, false otherwise
  2. true if ptr can be resolved to a value starting at this view, false otherwise

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
1. Linear in the number of members: as for ordered_json, members are compared one after another, in document order, stopping at the first match. Each comparison first checks the key's length — already known from the index, without reading the key bytes — before comparing its content. Objects with 128 or more members get a hash index of their keys while parsing, so that a lookup in them takes constant time on average.
  2. Linear in the number of reference tokens of ptr and, for each token, in the number of members of the object at that level or the index into the array — as for operator[] and at with a JSON pointer.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Duplicate keys: the first member wins

If the source text repeats a key, this resolves to the first member with it, not to the last one that materialize() and parse() keep. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[] and Duplicate keys for the reasons and for how to get the last value.

Overload 1 always returns false when the value is not an object — including a discarded view.

Postconditions

If v.contains(key) returns true, then v[key] is not discarded and v.at(key) does not throw. If v.contains(ptr) returns true, then v[ptr] is not discarded and v.at(ptr) does not throw.

Overload 2 never throws

Unlike BasicJsonType::contains(const json_pointer&), which can throw for certain malformed pointers (for instance an empty array-index reference token), overload 2 never throws: a missing key, an out-of-range or malformed array index, a "-" index, or a reference token used on a primitive all simply make it return false.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• find - find a value in an object
  • count - returns the number of occurrences of a key
  • at, operator[] - resolve a JSON pointer and throw, or return a discarded view
  • BasicJsonType::contains - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.text: • Added in version 3.13.0 unreleased.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::count
docs.text:
size_type count(string_view_t key) const;
size_type count(const char* key) const;
size_type count(const string_t& key) const;

Returns the number of members with key key if the value is an object, 0 otherwise. Members with a repeated key are all counted.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: key (in) key value of the element to count

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: the number of members of the object with key key (duplicates included), or 0 if the value is not an object or has no such member.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the number of members: unlike the lookup functions, count() does not stop at the first match, because it has to count every member with the key. Members are compared one after another, in document order. Each comparison first checks the key's length — already known from the index, without reading the key bytes — before comparing its content. The hash index of the keys of objects with 128 or more members does not help here, since every member is visited.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
This method always returns 0 when the value is not an object — including a discarded view.

If the source text repeats a key, count() returns more than 1 for it, even though the materialized value (like the result of parse()) would have only one member with that key. Hence count(key) > 1 detects duplicate keys. This is unlike the lookup functions (operator[], at, find, contains), which resolve to the first member; see the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[].

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• find - find a value in an object
  • contains - checks whether a key exists
  • BasicJsonType::count - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.text: • Added in version 3.13.0 unreleased.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::dump
docs.text:
string_t dump(const int indent = -1,
              const char indent_char = ' ',
              const bool ensure_ascii = false,
              const number_format numbers = number_format::shortest) const;

Serializes this value (and its subtree) directly from the flat index, without ever building a BasicJsonType value first. With the default numbers == number_format::shortest, the result is the same string BasicJsonType::dump would produce for the value BasicJsonType::parse() builds from the same source text, called with the same indent, indent_char, and ensure_ascii — except that members of an object appear in document order rather than sorted by key, and every occurrence of a repeated key is written rather than only the last one (see Notes on duplicate keys). For a json_view (whose BasicJsonType is not ordered), this means dump() can print an object's members in a different order than materialize().dump() of the same subtree.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: indent (in) If indent is nonnegative, array elements and object members are pretty-printed with that indent level. An indent level of 0 only inserts newlines. -1 (the default) selects the most compact representation. indent_char (in) The character used for indentation if indent is greater than 0. The default is (space). ensure_ascii (in) If ensure_ascii is true, all non-ASCII characters in the output are escaped with \uXXXX sequences, and the result consists of ASCII characters only. numbers (in) how to write numbers, see number_format: shortest (the default) writes them the way BasicJsonType::dump would; source copies every number exactly as it appears in the source text.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: string containing the serialization of this value, or "<discarded>" if the view is discarded.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong exception safety: if an exception is thrown, there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc if allocating the output string fails. Unlike BasicJsonType::dump, there is no error_handler parameter and no type_error.316: the view only ever holds text the parser already validated as UTF-8, so there is nothing to replace or ignore.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the size of the output text.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The walk over the subtree is iterative, so the nesting depth it can write is limited by available memory only, not by the call stack — as for materialize().

Strings are escaped by the same rules as BasicJsonType::dump.

With numbers == number_format::shortest, floats are written with the library's shortest round-trip conversion, exactly as BasicJsonType::dump would (e.g. 1.5, 100.0, 1e+100), and integers are copied from the source text — already canonical in JSON, so this matches their shortest form too — except that -0 is written as 0, the way BasicJsonType::parse() reads it.

number_format::source copies every number exactly as written in the source text instead, with no exception for -0 — 1.50, 1E2, -0.0, -0, or all digits of an integer literal with more digits than any number type holds (such a literal is itself classified as a float, see What is different) — something BasicJsonType cannot do, since parsing already reduces every number to its parsed value.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• number_format - how dump() writes numbers
  • operator<< - serialize this value to a stream
  • materialize - build a BasicJsonType value, e.g. to use BasicJsonType::dump's error_handler
  • BasicJsonType::dump - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • Zero-copy JSON views - writing a view back without building a tree

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::get
docs.text:
template<typename T>
T get() const;

Converts the value to T.

For the types below, the conversion works directly on the flat index — no BasicJsonType value is built for it:

  • bool
  • arithmetic types other than bool (for a boolean, 0/1, exactly as for BasicJsonType::get<T>())
  • std::nullptr_t
  • std::basic_string<char, Traits, Alloc> (including string_t) — a copy of the string
  • string_view_t — no copy: the returned view points into the document's source() text, or, for a string that contains escape sequences, into the document's own buffer of decoded strings (see get_string())
  • BasicJsonType — equivalent to materialize()
  • basic_json_view — returns *this
  • std::vector<U, A> of the types above — from an array, element by element, each converted with get<U>(); std::vector<basic_json_view> keeps a view of every element instead of a value
  • std::map<K, basic_json_view, C, A> and std::unordered_map<K, basic_json_view, H, E, A>, if K is constructible from a (const char*, std::size_t) pair — views of the members of an object; with a repeated key, the view of the last member is kept, as BasicJsonType::parse() keeps its value

A default-constructible T whose from_json() accepts views reads the view directly as well, without building a BasicJsonType value. This covers the library's own conversions of the standard library types — all other std::vectors, std::map/std::unordered_map (also with other key types), std::list, std::deque, std::set, std::forward_list, std::valarray, std::array, C arrays, std::pair, std::tuple, std::optional, enumerations, std::filesystem::path, ... -- which give the same values as materialize().get<T>() (from an object, a repeated key keeps the last value, as BasicJsonType::parse() does), as well as the types of the NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_* and NLOHMANN_DEFINE_DERIVED_TYPE_* macros and the enumerations of NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM, and any from_json() constrained to accept views, e.g. with is_json_view. A from_json() that also accepts types that are no JSON values at all, such as the unconstrained template<typename BasicJsonType> void from_json(const BasicJsonType&,T&) of arbitrary type conversions, is not called with a view: it may use BasicJsonType functions a view does not have. See Writing generic code.

Duplicate keys

Such a from_json() looks members up in the view, where a repeated key finds the first member, while materialize().get<T>() sees the last one, as BasicJsonType::parse() keeps it: for {"x":1,"x":2}, get<point>() reads x == 1. See Duplicate keys.

Every other T — user types whose from_json() is written for BasicJsonType only, types without a default constructor, std::tuples holding references, ... — is converted by materialize().get<T>(): the subtree is built into a real BasicJsonType value first (as BasicJsonType::parse() would), and converted from there exactly as BasicJsonType::get<T>() would convert it.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: T the type to convert the value to

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: the value, converted to T

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• For the directly-converted types listed above (other than BasicJsonType and basic_json_view, which never throw): throws type_error.302 if the value's type does not match T — the same exception, with the same message, that BasicJsonType::get<T>() throws for the same JSON type and T.
  • For std::vector<U, A>: throws type_error.302 if the value is not an array; otherwise, whatever converting an element to U throws.
  • For std::map/std::unordered_map of views: throws type_error.302 if the value is not an object.
  • For a T whose from_json() reads the view: whatever that from_json() throws; for the library's conversions and the macros, the same exceptions with the same messages as BasicJsonType::get<T>() of the same value.
  • For every other T: whatever materialize().get<T>() throws — typically type_error.302, or whatever a user-provided from_json() throws.

None of the exceptions thrown directly by this function or by a from_json() that reads the view (the first four bullets above) carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at. An exception thrown while converting through materialize() (the last bullet) is different: it is thrown by a real BasicJsonType value, so it does carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path if BasicJsonType was built with it enabled. That path is relative to the root of the view's subtree, because materialize() builds only the subtree (with parent pointers): it is empty if the failing value is the subtree's root itself, and it never is the path within the whole document.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• bool, arithmetic types, std::nullptr_t, string_view_t, basic_json_view: constant.
  • std::basic_string<char, Traits, Alloc>: constant, plus one allocation and a copy of the string's bytes.
  • BasicJsonType: linear in the size of the subtree, see materialize().
  • std::vector<U, A>: linear in the number of elements, times the complexity of converting one element to U.
  • std::map/std::unordered_map: linear in the number of members for walking them, plus the container's own insertion cost per member (logarithmic for std::map, amortized constant for std::unordered_map), times the complexity of converting one member to the mapped type.
  • a T whose from_json() reads the view: the cost of that from_json(); for the macros, linear in the number of members times the cost of a lookup, plus the cost of converting the members.
  • every other T: the cost of materialize() and of destroying the BasicJsonType value afterwards, plus that of BasicJsonType::get<T>().

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Floating-point values

A floating-point T is converted from the same digits the lexer would see during BasicJsonType::parse(), using the same conversion, so the result is bit-for-bit identical to BasicJsonType::parse(text).get<T>() for the same source text.

Duplicate keys

std::map/std::unordered_map conversions keep the last value of a repeated key, like materialize() and BasicJsonType::parse() do. This is the opposite of operator[]/at/find/contains, which resolve to the first occurrence (see the Notes on duplicate keys).

No pointers, references, or implicit conversion

Unlike BasicJsonType, basic_json_view has no stored value anywhere to hand out a pointer or a reference to, so it provides neither get_ptr(), get_ref(), nor operator ValueType(). get_string() (equivalently, get<string_view_t>()) is the zero-copy alternative for strings.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• get_to - convert and write into a passed value
  • get_string - the string, without a copy
  • number_token - a number's token text, without a copy
  • materialize - build the BasicJsonType value of this subtree
  • BasicJsonType::get - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • Zero-copy JSON views - which conversions avoid building a basic_json value

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::get_string
docs.text:
string_view_t get_string() const;

Returns the string value as a string_view_t, without copying it.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: The string, as a string_view_t that points either into the document's source() text (a string with no escape sequences), or into the document's own buffer of decoded strings (a string that contains escape sequences, such as "\n" or "\u00e9", which had to be decoded once when the document was parsed).

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Throws type_error.302 if the value is not a string; example: "type must be string, but is array".

This exception does not carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
basic_json_view has no BasicJsonType value stored anywhere, so unlike BasicJsonType, it has no get_ref() to hand out a reference to a stored string_t. get_string() (equivalently, get<string_view_t>()) is the zero-copy alternative: BasicJsonType::get_ref<const string_t&>() is its closest counterpart, except that it returns a view instead of a reference to a value that must already exist.

get_string() borrows the string: nothing is copied, whereas get<std::string>() copies it. For a borrowed document, the returned string_view_t is valid as long as the caller's buffer; for an owned one, as long as the document.

The returned string_view_t is valid exactly as long as the view that produced it — see the validity rules of basic_json_view — and, for a string with no escapes, for as long as the document's source text, which for a borrowed document must remain valid and unmodified for as long as the document exists, since floating-point values and unescaped strings are read from the source lazily.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::get_to
docs.text:
template<typename T>
T& get_to(T& v) const;

Converts the value to T and stores it in v, in one of three ways:

  • For the types that get<T>() converts directly — arithmetic types, bool, std::nullptr_t, string_view_t, std::basic_string, BasicJsonType, basic_json_view, vectors of these, and maps of views — v is assigned: v = get<T>().
  • For a type whose from_json() accepts views (see get<T>()), that from_json() is called with the view and the existing v, without building a BasicJsonType value.
  • For every other type, the subtree is built into a BasicJsonType value and materialize().get_to(v) is called, i.e. from_json() is invoked with the existing v, exactly as BasicJsonType::get_to() does.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: T the type to convert the value to

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: v (out) the variable to store the converted value in

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: v, allowing calls to chain

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text:
• For the directly converted types: strong exception safety. If an exception is thrown, v is not modified.
  • For every other type: as for BasicJsonType::get_to(). materialize() throws before v is touched, but a from_json() that throws may leave v partly modified.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• For the directly converted types: whatever get<T>() throws for the same value and T.
  • For every other type: whatever materialize() and BasicJsonType::get_to() throw.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
• For the directly converted types: whatever get<T>() has for the same T.
  • For every other type: that of materialize(), plus that of BasicJsonType::get_to().

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The difference between the two ways matters for a from_json() that sets only the fields present in the JSON: since it runs on the existing v, the other fields of v keep their values, whereas assigning get<T>() would replace them with those of a default-constructed T.

docs.title: Examples
See also

• get - convert the value to a given type
  • BasicJsonType::get_to - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • Zero-copy JSON views - which conversions avoid building a basic_json value

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::is_array

bool is_binary() const noexcept;

This function always returns false: a document is only ever parsed from JSON text, never from CBOR or the other binary formats, and a JSON text has no binary values, so a view can never refer to one. The function exists for interface parity with BasicJsonType::is_binary.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::is_discarded
docs.text:
bool is_discarded() const noexcept;

Returns whether this view is invalid, i.e. does not refer to a value. This is the case for a default-constructed view (see (constructor)), and for root() of a document that is itself discarded — in particular, the root of a failed parse() with allow_exceptions set to false.

A discarded view is also what operator[] returns for a missing key, an index out of range, or a JSON pointer that cannot be resolved, and for any access on a view that is itself discarded (so a chain such as v["a"]["b"] is safe). at throws instead.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: true if the view or its document is discarded, false otherwise.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: A basic_json_view is not convertible to bool: such a conversion would mean "refers to a value", whereas basic_json converts to the bool it holds, so the same code would silently behave differently. Test !v.is_discarded() explicitly.

docs.title: Examples
See also

• operator[] - access specified element; yields a discarded view where an element is missing
  • (constructor) - the default constructor creates a discarded view
  • basic_json_document::is_discarded - return whether the last parse failed
  • BasicJsonType::is_discarded - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • Zero-copy JSON views - how views differ from basic_json

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::items
docs.text:
/* unspecified */ items() const noexcept;

Returns a range of items — (key, value) pairs — for use in range-based for loops. An item's key() is a string_view_t (for an array element, its index converted to a string, as for BasicJsonType::items()), and its value() is a basic_json_view of the element.

The returned type is not part of the public API and may change between versions; use a range-based for loop (see the example), or decltype(v.items()) if you need to name it.

for (const auto& item : v.items())
{
    std::cout << "key: " << item.key() << ", value: " << item.value() << '\n';
}

On C++17, item also supports structured bindings:

for (const auto [key, value] : v.items())
{
    std::cout << "key: " << key << ", value: " << value << '\n';
}

Note the const auto (by value), not const auto&: unlike BasicJsonType::items(), whose elements are references into an existing object, a view's item is produced on the fly for each step of the iteration, so there is nothing for a reference to bind to.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: A range whose iterators dereference to an item (with key() and value(), see above) and whose begin()/end() are equivalent to basic_json_view::begin()/end(), in document order.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
As for begin()/end(), items() visits every member of an object, including all occurrences of a duplicate key — unlike operator[], at, find, and contains, which resolve to the first member with a given key. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[].

Lifetime issues

Unlike BasicJsonType::items() (see #2040), calling items() on a temporary view is safe, for instance for (auto item : v["a"].items()): the returned range holds a copy of the view. What must outlive the loop is the document and, for a borrowed document, the source buffer.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• begin, end - the iterators items() is built on
  • BasicJsonType::items - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::materialize
docs.text:
BasicJsonType materialize() const;

Builds the BasicJsonType value of this subtree: the value BasicJsonType::parse() would have produced for the same source text, allocated for the first time by this call.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: The BasicJsonType value of this subtree, or a discarded BasicJsonType value (BasicJsonType(value_t::discarded)) if the view is discarded.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to (nothing about either is mutated by this function).

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc (via BasicJsonType's allocator) if constructing the result fails.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the size of the subtree.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
materialize() replays the subtree through the same SAX builder BasicJsonType::parse() uses, so the result matches it exactly — including, for an object, that a repeated key keeps only its last value. The replay is iterative, so it is not limited by the call stack the way a naive recursive conversion would be; the JSON nesting depth is limited only by available memory, as for BasicJsonType::parse() itself.

Unlike parsing with JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS enabled, the values produced by materialize() do not carry source positions. The index has the start offset of every value, but not the end of arrays, objects, and escaped strings, which the positions also need.

Calling materialize() on the same view repeatedly builds a new, independent BasicJsonType value each time; it never caches the result.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• root - the view of a document's root value
  • BasicJsonType::parse - build a BasicJsonType value directly from a JSON text
  • JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS - source positions on parsed values (not produced by materialize())
  • Zero-copy JSON views - when to build a basic_json value from a view

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::number_format
docs.text:
enum class number_format {
    shortest,
    source
};

This enumeration is used in dump to choose how numbers are written. Two values are differentiated:

shortest integers are copied from the source text — already canonical in JSON — except that -0 becomes 0, the way BasicJsonType::parse() reads it; floats are written with the library's shortest round-trip conversion, exactly as BasicJsonType::dump() would (e.g. 1.5, 100.0, 1e+100) source every number is copied exactly as it appears in the source text — 1.50, 1E2, -0, all digits of an integer literal with more digits than any number type holds — something BasicJsonType cannot do, since parsing already reduces every number to its parsed value

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• dump - serialize to a JSON-formatted string
  • number_token - get a single number's token text without dumping the whole value
  • BasicJsonType::error_handler_t - the analogous enumeration for BasicJsonType::dump's decoding-error behavior
  • Zero-copy JSON views - writing numbers as they appeared in the source

docs.title: Version history
docs.text: • Added in version 3.13.0 unreleased.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::number_token
docs.text:
string_view_t number_token() const;

Returns the number exactly as it appears in the source text, without parsing or rounding it.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: The number's token text, as a string_view_t into the document's source() text — for example "1.50", "1E2", "-0", or an integer literal with more digits than any number type holds (such as a 30-digit integer, which get<T>() and materialize() can only represent approximately, as a number_float_t).

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Throws type_error.302 if the value is not a number; example: "type must be number, but is string".

This exception does not carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
BasicJsonType has no counterpart to this function: once a number is parsed into number_integer_t, number_unsigned_t, or number_float_t, its original textual form (leading zeros aside, which are already rejected by the grammar; trailing zeros in the fraction; the case and sign of the exponent; ...) is gone. number_token() is useful precisely where that form must survive — a price or an identifier that must be reproduced exactly, or a number too large for any of BasicJsonType's number types to hold without loss.

The returned string_view_t always points into the document's source() text — numbers are never decoded into the document's separate string buffer — and is valid exactly as long as that text is, see the validity rules of basic_json_view.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• get - convert the value to a given type
  • get_string - the string, without a copy
  • BasicJsonType::number_integer_t, number_unsigned_t, number_float_t - the number types get<T>() and materialize() convert into
  • Zero-copy JSON views - reading a number exactly as written

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::operator[]
docs.text:
// (1)
basic_json_view operator[](string_view_t key) const;
basic_json_view operator[](const char* key) const;
basic_json_view operator[](const string_t& key) const;

// (2)
basic_json_view operator[](size_type idx) const;
template<typename IntegerType>
basic_json_view operator[](IntegerType idx) const;

// (3)
basic_json_view operator[](const json_pointer& ptr) const;
  1. Returns the value of the object member with key key — the first one, should the key occur more than once (see the Notes below) — or a discarded view if there is no such member.
  2. Returns the array element at index idx, or a discarded view if idx is out of range. The template accepts every integer type except bool and std::size_t (int, unsigned, long, std::int64_t, ...) and forwards to the size_type overload, so that an integer argument is not ambiguous between that overload and 1; a negative idx is out of range.
  3. Returns the value a JSON pointer ptr refers to, starting at this value, or a discarded view wherever resolving it further is not possible without inserting into or extending the document (see Return value and Exceptions below).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: key (in) object key of the element to access idx (in) index of the element to access ptr (in) JSON pointer to the element to access

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
1. the value of the first member with key key, or a discarded view if no member has this key (or if this view is discarded)
  2. the element at index idx, or a discarded view if idx >= size() or idx is negative (or if this view is discarded)
  3. the value ptr resolves to, starting at this value, or a discarded view (also if this view is discarded) for exactly the reference tokens where the const overload of BasicJsonType::operator[] invokes undefined behavior for the same pointer and the same document: an object member that does not exist, or an array index that is out of range

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
1. Throws type_error.305 if the value is not an object and not discarded — the same exception, with the same message, that the const overload of BasicJsonType::operator[] throws for a string argument on a non-object value.
  2. Throws type_error.305 if the value is not an array and not discarded — the same exception, with the same message, that the const overload of BasicJsonType::operator[] throws for a numeric argument on a non-array value.
  3. Throws the same exceptions, with the same messages, that the const overload of BasicJsonType::operator[] throws for the same pointer and the same document:
    • out_of_range.402 if a reference token is "-" at an array.
    • out_of_range.404 if a reference token cannot be resolved because it is used on a primitive value.
    • parse_error.106 if an array index in ptr begins with '0'.
    • parse_error.109 if an array index in ptr is not a number.

None of these exceptions carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
1. Linear in the number of members: as for ordered_json, members are compared one after another, in document order, stopping at the first match. Each comparison first checks the key's length — already known from the index, without reading the key bytes — before comparing its content, so a key of a different length than key is rejected without touching the source text. Objects with 128 or more members get a hash index of their keys while parsing, so that a lookup in them takes constant time on average.
  2. Linear in idx: elements are skipped one at a time from the first one, since they are not a fixed size in the index (unlike BasicJsonType's array, which is random-access). Constant if no element of the array is an array or object, since the elements are then adjacent in the index.
  3. Linear in the number of reference tokens of ptr and, for each token, in the number of members of the object at that level (as 1.) or the index into the array (as 2.).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Unlike BasicJsonType::operator[], which is undefined behavior (guarded by a runtime assertion) for a missing key on a const value, this operator returns a safe, testable result for a missing key or an index out of range: a discarded view, which is tested with is_discarded. There is also no non-const overload that inserts a missing key or extends an array — a view never modifies the document.

Chained access

operator[] on a discarded view returns a discarded view and does not throw, so a chain like v["a"]["b"][0] is safe even if "a" or "b" is missing: the first missing step makes the whole result discarded, which is tested once at the end. Type errors on values that are not discarded still throw: a key on an array or a primitive, or an index on an object or a primitive, is type_error.305 as for BasicJsonType. at still throws for a discarded view, as it does for a missing key.

Duplicate keys: the first member wins

If the source text has an object with a duplicate key, operator[] (and at, find, contains, value, and JSON pointer resolution) all resolve to the first member with that key, because a lookup can stop as soon as it finds a match. This is different from materialize() (and BasicJsonType::parse()), which replay every member in order and so keep the last value for a repeated key, so v["a"] and v.materialize()["a"] can differ. To get the value parse() would give, use materialize() or iterate the members with items() and keep the last match. The key hash index of a larger object (128 members or more) leads to the first member of a key as well. begin()/end() and items() iterate over all members, including duplicates, in document order. See Duplicate keys and size().

JSON pointer resolution

Overload 3 walks ptr one reference token at a time, starting at this value, the same way at and contains do. It only ever returns a discarded view where the const overload of BasicJsonType::operator[] would be undefined behavior for the same pointer — a missing object member or an out-of-range array index — and still throws for every other way ptr can fail to resolve. See at for the checked version, which throws in every case instead, and contains for a version that never throws.

See also
docs.text:
• at - access specified element with bounds checking (throws instead of returning a discarded view)
  • front, back - access the first or last element
  • find, contains - look up a member without throwing
  • BasicJsonType::operator[] - the corresponding function of basic_json
  • json_pointer - JSON pointer type used by overload 3

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::operator==
docs.text:
// (1)
bool operator==(const basic_json_view& lhs, const basic_json_view& rhs);

// (2)
bool operator==(const basic_json_view& lhs, const BasicJsonType& rhs);
bool operator==(const BasicJsonType& lhs, const basic_json_view& rhs);
  1. Compares two views for equality: whether the values BasicJsonType::parse() would produce for lhs and rhs are equal, according to BasicJsonType's operator==.
  2. Compares a view and a BasicJsonType value for equality, in either order: whether the value parse() would produce for the view and the other operand are equal, according to BasicJsonType's operator==.

Neither overload builds a BasicJsonType value for a view to do the comparison (see Notes below). Numbers compare by value across their types (1 == 1.0), and an object compares by its members, with duplicate keys resolved exactly as parse() resolves them — the last value, at the position of the first occurrence of the key. This is not what operator[] and the other lookups return for a duplicate key: they find the first member (see Duplicate keys).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: lhs (in) first value to consider rhs (in) second value to consider

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: whether the values lhs and rhs are equal

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong exception safety: if an exception is thrown, there are no changes to either operand, or to the document(s) a view refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc. Unlike the other comparison and most other basic_json_view functions, operator== is not noexcept: resolving an object's members needs a temporary array to sort them by key (see Complexity below), and that allocation can fail.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the size of the compared values: every number, string, array element, and object member is visited at most once, and the walk is iterative, so the nesting depth it can compare is limited by available memory only, not by the call stack (as for materialize()). Resolving an object's members takes an additional O(n log n) in the number of members at that level, since they are sorted by key to detect and resolve duplicates before being compared. Two arrays of different size() are rejected without visiting either one's elements.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Only a single number, boolean, or null value is ever materialized into a BasicJsonType, to reuse its operator== — for numbers, so that values written differently in the source text but equal in value (e.g. an integer and a floating-point literal) still compare equal, following the same rules BasicJsonType does for special values such as NaN. Constructing one of these scalars never allocates. Strings are compared directly, without allocating, either from the source text on both sides or, for overload 2, against BasicJsonType's own string. Arrays and objects are never materialized at all; only their elements or members are visited, one pair at a time.

How objects are compared

For a json_view (BasicJsonType::object_t is std::map), members are compared by key, regardless of the order they appear in the source text. For an ordered_json_view (object_t is ordered_map), they are compared in the order they occur, so the very same two objects with their members reordered can compare equal as json_views but not as ordered_json_views. This is exactly how json and ordered_json compare, see "Comparing different basic_json specializations".

Discarded views

A discarded view compares the same way a discarded BasicJsonType value does, which is governed by JSON_USE_LEGACY_DISCARDED_VALUE_COMPARISON: by default, a discarded view is never equal to anything, not even another discarded view.

No ordering comparison (operator<) is provided for basic_json_view; materialize() is the way to get a BasicJsonType value that supports it.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• operator!= - compare for inequality
  • materialize - build a BasicJsonType value, e.g. to keep comparing after the document is gone
  • BasicJsonType::operator== - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::operator<<
docs.text:
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& o, const basic_json_view& v);

Not available when JSON_NO_IO is defined.

Serializes the given view v to the output stream o, using dump — exactly as operator<<(std::ostream&, const basic_json&) does for a basic_json value.

  • The indentation of the output can be controlled with the member variable width of the output stream o. For instance, using the manipulator std::setw(4) on o sets the indentation level to 4, and the serialization result is the same as calling v.dump(4). A width of 0 or less (the default) selects the most compact representation, as v.dump(-1) does.
  • The indentation character can be controlled with the member variable fill of the output stream o. For instance, the manipulator std::setfill('\t') sets indentation to use a tab character rather than the default space character.
  • As for basic_json, o's width is reset to 0 after this call, whether or not it was greater than 0 before.

Numbers are always written as v.dump() writes them by default, i.e. as with number_format::shortest; there is no way to select number_format::source through the stream.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: o (in, out) stream to write to v (in) view to serialize

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: the stream o

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc, propagated from dump. Unlike operator<<(std::ostream&, const basic_json&), there is no UTF-8 decoding step that could throw type_error.316, and no error_handler to choose between — see the Exceptions of dump.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear, as dump.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• dump - serialize to a JSON-formatted string
  • operator<<(std::ostream&) - the corresponding operator for basic_json
  • JSON_NO_IO - switch off functions relying on certain C++ I/O headers
  • Zero-copy JSON views - writing a view back without building a tree

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::operator!=
docs.text:
// (1)
bool operator!=(const basic_json_view& lhs, const basic_json_view& rhs);

// (2)
bool operator!=(const basic_json_view& lhs, const BasicJsonType& rhs);
bool operator!=(const BasicJsonType& lhs, const basic_json_view& rhs);
  1. Compares two views for inequality. Returns !(lhs == rhs), see operator==.
  2. Compares a view and a BasicJsonType value for inequality, in either order. Returns !(lhs == rhs) (or, for the reversed order, !(rhs == lhs)), see operator==.

Since operator!= is defined as the negation of operator==, it follows the same rules for special cases: for instance, since a discarded view is never equal to anything by default (see operator=='s Notes), it is never unequal to anything either — discarded != discarded is also false, exactly as for a discarded BasicJsonType value.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: lhs (in) first value to consider rhs (in) second value to consider

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: whether the values lhs and rhs are not equal

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong exception safety: if an exception is thrown, there are no changes to either operand, or to the document(s) a view refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: May throw std::bad_alloc, propagated from operator==. Unlike most other basic_json_view functions, operator!= is not noexcept.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear, as operator==.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
See the Notes of operator== — in particular for how an object's members are compared (order matters for ordered_json_view but not for json_view) and for how discarded views compare.

No ordering comparison (operator<) is provided for basic_json_view; materialize() is the way to get a BasicJsonType value that supports it.

docs.text:

  • materialize - build a BasicJsonType value, e.g. to keep comparing after the document is gone
  • BasicJsonType::operator!= - the corresponding function of basic_json

size_type size() const noexcept;

Returns the number of elements, as BasicJsonType::size() would for the same value.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
The return value depends on the type and is defined as follows:

Value type return value null 0 discarded 0 boolean 1 string 1 number 1 object number of key/value pairs array number of elements

docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant: for an object or array, the element count is stored in the index, not counted on demand.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
As for BasicJsonType::size(), this does not return the length of a string value — it is 1 for a string, regardless of its length.

If the source text has an object with a duplicate key, every occurrence counts towards its size() — unlike materialize() (and BasicJsonType::parse()), which keeps only the last value for a repeated key. This means v.size() can be larger than v.materialize().size(). See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[] for why lookups and iteration disagree on how many members there are.

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::source_offset
docs.text:
std::size_t source_offset() const noexcept;

Returns the byte offset of this value in the document's source() text, without materializing anything.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
• For a string with no escapes, a number, true/false/null, an array, or an object: the byte offset of the first byte of the value's token (for a string: the first byte after the opening quote) in source().
  • static_cast<std::size_t>(-1) for a discarded view, and for a string that contains escapes — such a string was decoded once into the document's own buffer, so there is no single byte range in source() left to point at.

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Constant.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This is a raw offset, not a length: the API does not (yet) expose how many bytes the token occupies in the source text, so source_offset() alone is enough to report where a value came from (for an error message, for syntax highlighting, ...) but not to slice its exact text back out of source() for a string, whose token length is not the same as its decoded size().

docs.title: nlohmann::basic_json_view::value
docs.text:
// (1)
template<typename T>
T value(string_view_t key, const T& default_value) const;
string_t value(string_view_t key, const char* default_value) const;

// (2)
template<typename T>
T value(const json_pointer& ptr, const T& default_value) const;
string_t value(const json_pointer& ptr, const char* default_value) const;
  1. Returns the value of the object member with key key — the first one, should the key occur more than once (see Notes on duplicate keys) — converted to T, or default_value if there is no such member.
  2. Returns the value a JSON pointer ptr refers to, starting at this value, converted to T, or default_value if ptr cannot be resolved.

Both overloads have a dedicated const char* overload, so v.value(key, "default") (and the JSON pointer equivalent) deduce string_t, not const char*, for their return type and for the comparison used to pick between key and default_value.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: T the type to convert the found value to; also the type of default_value

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: key (in) object key of the element to access ptr (in) JSON pointer to the element to access default_value (in) the value to return if key/ptr resolves to no value

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
1. the first member with key key, converted to T, or default_value
  2. the value ptr resolves to, converted to T, or default_value

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: Strong guarantee: there are no changes to the view or the document it refers to.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
1. Throws type_error.306 if the value is not an object — the same exception, with the same message, that BasicJsonType::value throws for the same call. If a member with key key is found, throws whatever converting it to T throws (typically type_error.302, with the same message BasicJsonType::value throws for the same mismatch); a missing member never throws.
  2. Throws type_error.306 if this value — not the value ptr resolves to — is neither an object nor an array. Throws parse_error.106 or parse_error.109 if ptr contains a malformed array index. If ptr resolves to a value, throws whatever converting it to T throws. Every other way ptr can fail to resolve — a missing key, an out-of-range or "-" array index, an unresolvable token on a primitive — yields default_value instead of throwing, exactly as BasicJsonType::value catches out_of_range and returns default_value.

None of these exceptions carry a JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path: the view has no BasicJsonType value to point at, so the exception is created without one, even if BasicJsonType was built with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS enabled.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text:
1. Linear in the number of members: as for operator[], members are compared one after another, in document order, stopping at the first match. Plus the complexity of converting the found member to T (see get). Objects with 128 or more members get a hash index of their keys while parsing, so that a lookup in them takes constant time on average.
  2. Linear in the number of reference tokens of ptr and, for each token, in the number of members of the object at that level or the index into the array — as for the operator[] and at overloads that take a JSON pointer. Plus the complexity of converting the resolved value to T.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Duplicate keys: the first member wins

If the source text repeats a key, this resolves to the first member with it, not to the last one that materialize() and parse() keep. See the Notes on duplicate keys of operator[] and Duplicate keys for the reasons and for how to get the last value.

Differences to at and operator[]

Unlike at, this function does not throw if key/ptr resolves to no value. Unlike operator[], it never returns a discarded view — it always returns a T — and it is available on any view, since it never needs to insert a missing element the way the non-const BasicJsonType::operator[] would.

Which values can be asked

As for BasicJsonType::value, the key overload (1) requires an object, and the JSON pointer overload (2) an object or an array.

docs.title: Examples
See also
docs.text:
• at - access specified element with bounds checking (throws instead of returning a default value)
  • operator[] - access specified element (returns a discarded view instead of a default value)
  • BasicJsonType::value - the corresponding function of basic_json

docs.title: nlohmann::json_pointer
docs.text:
template<typename RefStringType>
class json_pointer;

A JSON pointer defines a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JSON document. It can be used with functions at and operator[]. Furthermore, JSON pointers are the base for JSON patches.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text:
RefStringType the string type used for the reference tokens making up the JSON pointer

Deprecation

For backwards compatibility RefStringType may also be a specialization of basic_json in which case string_t will be deduced as basic_json::string_t. This feature is deprecated and may be removed in a future major version.

See the migration guide for how to update existing code.

A JSON pointer is internally a sequence of reference tokens. front, pop_front, and push_front act on the first reference token, whereas back, pop_back, and push_back act on the last one. parent_pointer returns a new JSON pointer with the last reference token removed (like a non-mutating pop_back):

flowchart LR
    A["a"] --> B["b"] --> C["c"]

    front["front() / pop_front() / push_front()"] -.-> A
    back["back() / pop_back() / push_back()"] -.-> C
    parent["parent_pointer() returns /a/b"] -.-> B

Boxes are the reference tokens in order; dotted arrows show which token each member function reads, removes, or adds to.

The diagram shows the reference tokens of the JSON pointer /a/b/c.

docs.text: • string_t - the string type used for the reference tokens

docs.title: nlohmann::json_pointer::operator==
docs.text:
// until C++20
template<typename RefStringTypeLhs, typename RefStringTypeRhs>
bool operator==(
    const json_pointer<RefStringTypeLhs>& lhs,
    const json_pointer<RefStringTypeRhs>& rhs) noexcept;            // (1)

template<typename RefStringTypeLhs, typename StringType>
bool operator==(
    const json_pointer<RefStringTypeLhs>& lhs,
    const StringType& rhs);                                         // (2)

template<typename RefStringTypeRhs, typename StringType>
bool operator==(
    const StringType& lhs,
    const json_pointer<RefStringTypeRhs>& rhs);                     // (2)

// since C++20
template<typename RefStringTypeRhs>
bool operator==(
    const json_pointer<RefStringTypeRhs>& rhs) const noexcept;      // (1)

bool operator==(const string_t& rhs) const;                         // (2)

  1. Compares two JSON pointers for equality by comparing their reference tokens.

  2. Compares a JSON pointer and a string or a string and a JSON pointer for equality by converting the string to a JSON pointer and comparing the JSON pointers according to 1.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: RefStringTypeLhs, RefStringTypeRhs the string type of the left-hand side or right-hand side JSON pointer, respectively StringType the string type derived from the json_pointer operand (json_pointer::string_t)

docs.title: Parameters

docs.title: Return value

docs.title: nlohmann::json_pointer::operator<=>
docs.text:
// since C++20
template<typename RefStringTypeRhs>
std::strong_ordering operator<=>(const json_pointer<RefStringTypeRhs>& rhs) const noexcept; // *NOPAD*

3-way compares two JSON pointers by lexicographically comparing their sequences of reference tokens: corresponding reference tokens are compared with string_t's own operator<=>, and the first pair of tokens that differs determines the result. If all corresponding reference tokens compare equal, the JSON pointer with fewer reference tokens is ordered first.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: RefStringTypeRhs the string type of the right-hand side JSON pointer

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: rhs (in) JSON pointer to compare *this with

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: the std::strong_ordering of the 3-way comparison of *this and rhs

docs.title: Exception safety
docs.text: No-throw guarantee: this function never throws exceptions.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear in the number of reference tokens.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Ordering enables use as an associative container key

Together with operator==, operator<=> makes json_pointer a LessThanComparable type, so it can be used as the key type of ordered associative containers such as std::map or std::set.

Before C++20

Without C++20's three-way comparison, json_pointer provides a non-member operator< instead, which orders JSON pointers the same way. JSON pointers can therefore be used as keys of ordered associative containers with any supported C++ standard.

docs.title: nlohmann::json_sax
docs.text:
template<typename BasicJsonType>
struct json_sax;

This class describes the SAX interface used by sax_parse. Each function is called in different situations while the input is parsed. The boolean return value informs the parser whether to continue processing the input.

For instance, parsing the JSON text {"a": [1, true]} triggers the following callbacks, in order:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parser
    participant H as SAX handler

    P->>H: start_object(elements)
    P->>H: key("a")
    P->>H: start_array(elements)
    P->>H: number_unsigned(1)
    P->>H: boolean(true)
    P->>H: end_array()
    P->>H: end_object()

Each arrow is one call from the parser to the SAX handler, from top to bottom in the order the calls happen.

Note elements is passed as std::numeric_limits<std::size_t>::max() (i.e., "unknown") for JSON text input; only binary formats such as CBOR or MessagePack may report the actual number of elements in start_object/ start_array. Also note that 1 is reported via number_unsigned rather than number_integer because it has no leading - sign.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
• JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN - read a std::istream one character at a time instead of scanning its stream buffer in bulk
  • JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO - read a FILE* with std::fgetc instead of locking it once and using the unlocked stdio functions
  • JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION - opt in to leaving an input stream positioned right after a parsed number
  • JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8 - opt in to checking strings for valid UTF-8 in the CBOR, UBJSON, BJData, and BSON writers
  • JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING - opt in to rejecting a NUL byte in the input instead of treating it as end of input

docs.title: Language support
docs.text:
• JSON_HAS_CPP_11JSON_HAS_CPP_14JSON_HAS_CPP_17JSON_HAS_CPP_20 - set supported C++ standard
  • JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEMJSON_HAS_EXPERIMENTAL_FILESYSTEM - control std::filesystem support
  • JSON_HAS_RANGE_VIEW_CONVERSION - control construction from std::ranges views
  • JSON_HAS_RANGES - control std::ranges support
  • JSON_HAS_STATIC_RTTI - control RTTI (run time type information) support
  • JSON_HAS_STD_FORMAT - control std::format/std::formatter support
  • JSON_HAS_THREE_WAY_COMPARISON - control 3-way comparison support
  • JSON_NO_AUTOMATIC_UDLS - do not include the user-defined string literals (UDLs) automatically
  • JSON_NO_IO - switch off functions relying on certain C++ I/O headers
  • JSON_NO_SIMD - use only portable code instead of vector instructions (SSE2, SSSE3, NEON)
