docs.title: Zero-copy JSON views
docs.text: <nlohmann/json_view.hpp> adds a read-only, non-owning way to look at a parsed JSON text, as an alternative to building a basic_json tree with parse().

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: basic_json::parse() builds a tree of basic_json values: one allocation for every array and object, and every string copied into its own std::string. That is the right trade-off when the program goes on to read and write the value freely, but it does more work than necessary when only a small part of a large JSON text is actually needed, or when the same text is parsed over and over (many small messages, for instance) and most of the resulting tree is thrown away almost immediately.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
basic_json_document::parse() parses the same JSON grammar, with the same options, but instead of a tree it builds a flat index of the values it found: one 16-byte entry per value (and one per object key), in document order. Integers are converted while parsing and stored in their entry. Floating-point numbers and strings are referenced in place in the source text: a float is converted when it is read, and only strings that contain escape sequences are decoded, into one shared buffer owned by the document.

basic_json_view is a small, trivially copyable handle (two pointers) into that index. It gives you the read-only, type-inspection part of the basic_json interface — type() and the is_*() predicates, size()/empty() — as well as element access (operator[], at, front/back), lookup (find, contains, count), and iteration (begin/end, items) — without ever allocating a basic_json value. When you do need an actual basic_json value for a subtree, materialize() builds exactly the one parse() would have produced for it.

The same small text, parsed both ways:

The same J​SON text parsed by basic_json::parse() and by json_document::parse() The text {"port": 6379, "price": 19.90, "tags": ["eu", "a\"b"]}. Top: basic_json::parse() builds a tree: the root json value points to a std::map whose three nodes are separate heap allocations; the price is stored as the double 19.9; the tags array is a std::vector of two json values, each pointing to its own std::string. Bottom: json_document::parse() keeps the 54 bytes of source text and builds a flat index of nine 16-byte nodes in document order: object, key port, unsigned integer 6379 (the converted value is in the node), key price, float, key tags, array, string eu, and an escaped string. Keys, the float, and the plain string point back into the source text; the escaped string points into the document's buffer of decoded strings. A json_view is two pointers: one to the document and one to a node, here the array. basic_json::parse(): a tree, every array, object, and string in its own heap allocation json std::map "port" 6379 "price" 19.9 double: 19.90 is gone "tags" • std::vector json json std::string eu std::string a"b a separate heap allocation json_document::parse(): the source text stays where it is; one flat index of 16-byte nodes source text, 54 bytes (borrowed, or owned by the document) { " p o r t " : 6 3 7 9 , " p r i c e " : 1 9 . 9 0 , " t a g s " : [ " e u " , " a \ " b " ] } 0 10 20 30 40 50 json_document: owns the node index and the buffer of decoded strings node index: 9 nodes × 16 bytes = 144 bytes, in document order 0 object len 3 next 9 1 key off 2 len 4 2 uint 6379 (converted) 3 key off 16 len 5 4 float off 24 len 5 5 key off 32 len 4 6 array len 2 next 3 7 string off 41 len 2 8 string escaped len 3 decoded strings a " b json_view v = doc.root()["tags"] doc* node* integers are converted while parsing and kept in their node; floats and strings point back into the text

Top: the tree of separate heap allocations that basic_json::parse() builds. Bottom: json_document::parse() keeps the source text and builds one flat index of 16-byte nodes that point back into it, plus a buffer of decoded strings.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp> in addition to (or instead of) <nlohmann/json.hpp>. Parse into a json_document, inspect its root(), and materialize() when you need a real value. materialize() works on any view, not just the root, so you can turn just the subtree you need into a value:

Example: parse a document, inspect its root, and materialize it 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

using nlohmann::json_document;

int main()
{
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;

    // json_document is basic_json_document<nlohmann::json>: same value types
    // and containers as the ordinary json specialization
    json_document doc = json_document::parse(R"({"pi": 3.14, "numbers": [1, 2, 3]})");

    std::cout << doc.root().is_object() << '\n';
    std::cout << doc.root().materialize().dump() << '\n';
}

Output:

true
{"numbers":[1,2,3],"pi":3.14}

ordered_json_document is the equivalent for ordered_json, just as ordered_json is to json.

docs.title: Ownership and lifetime
docs.text:
A document either borrows the text it was parsed from, or owns its own copy of it; call owns_source() to find out which happened. parse() decides this from the value category and type of its argument (an lvalue std::string is borrowed; an rvalue std::string is moved in, owned without a copy; a stream is read into an owned buffer; and so on — see parse's Notes for the full table). parse_copy() always owns a copy, regardless of the input.

A borrowed document depends on your buffer

If a document borrows its text, that text must outlive the document (and every view taken from it) and must stay unmodified for as long as the document exists, since floating-point values and unescaped strings are read from it lazily. Reading or writing through a view after the underlying buffer is gone is undefined behavior, exactly as it would be for a dangling std::string_view.

A view is valid only while all of the following hold:

  • the document is alive,
  • the document has not been re-parsed since the view was taken (with read() or parse() into it),
  • the document has not had shrink_to_fit() called on it since, and
  • if the document borrows its source text, that text is still alive and unmodified.

Moving the basic_json_document<> itself is fine and does not invalidate its views: the index is a separate heap allocation that keeps its address across the move. Take a fresh view from root() whenever any of the other conditions above was not met.

When a json_view becomes invalid Four timelines. First: a document borrows a std::string; when the string is destroyed, the document and every view taken from it dangle. Second: doc.read() re-parses the document; views taken before are invalid, a fresh view from root() is valid. Third: doc.shrink_to_fit() has the same effect. Fourth: moving the document does not invalidate its views; destroying the moved-to document does. alive / valid dangling: using it is undefined behavior time → The borrowed text is destroyed std::string text json_document doc json_view v text destroyed every view, and the document itself The document is re-parsed json_document doc json_view v v = doc.root() doc.read(other) views taken before a fresh view is valid again The document is shrunk json_document doc json_view v v = doc.root() doc.shrink_to_fit() views taken before a fresh view is valid again The document is moved, then destroyed json_document doc moved = std::move(doc) json_view v std::move: views stay valid moved is destroyed

Four timelines of a document and its views, each bar showing when an object is alive or valid and when it dangles. Destroying the borrowed text, re-parsing, or shrinking the document invalidates the views taken before; moving the document does not.

A view can dangle, exactly like a std::string_view: nothing stops you from using it after its document is gone. This is deliberate. A view is two pointers and trivially copyable; making it safe (a std::shared_ptr in the document and a std::weak_ptr in each view) would make it larger, add reference counting to every copy, and a lock() to every access — exactly the costs the view exists to avoid. What is caught is the obvious case: because a view dies with its document, root() is not callable on a temporary document: auto v = json_document::parse(text).root(); does not compile. Give the document a name first.

Example: borrowed and owned documents, and when views become invalid 
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

using nlohmann::json_document;

int main()
{
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;

    // BORROWED: doc only points into `text`; `text` must outlive `doc`
    std::string text = R"({"a": 1})";
    json_document doc = json_document::parse(text);
    std::cout << doc.owns_source() << '\n'; // false

    // a view is valid as long as the document is alive, has not been
    // re-parsed (read()) or shrunk (shrink_to_fit()), and -- if borrowed --
    // the source text is alive
    nlohmann::json_view v = doc.root();
    std::cout << v.is_object() << '\n';

    // re-parsing the SAME document invalidates views taken before the call;
    // `v` above must not be used after this line
    doc.read(R"([1, 2, 3])");
    v = doc.root(); // take a fresh view instead
    std::cout << v.is_array() << '\n';

    // moving the document does not invalidate views: the node index is
    // heap-allocated and does not move with the document object
    json_document moved = std::move(doc);
    std::cout << v.is_array() << '\n';
}

Output:

false
true
true
true

docs.title: What is the same as parse()
docs.text:
• Accept/reject. accept() and parse() accept and reject exactly the same inputs as basic_json::accept()/basic_json::parse(), with the same ignore_comments and ignore_trailing_commas options.
  • Errors. A failing parse throws the same exception — the same id, message, and position — because on failure the library's own parser is run on the same bytes to produce the diagnostic. Valid input never pays for this, and the replay builds no values: it costs about a lexing pass up to the error. allow_exceptions == false skips the replay and gives a discarded document instead of throwing, just as it gives a discarded value for basic_json::parse().
  • Number classification. An integer literal that does not fit into the 64-bit integer type becomes a floating-point value, exactly as it does for basic_json::parse().
  • Macros. JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING and JSON_NOEXCEPTION/JSON_THROW_USER behave the same way they do for <nlohmann/json.hpp>. These are the macros that change what the parser accepts or how it reports errors. The others either do not apply (JSON_DIAGNOSTICS needs parent pointers in basic_json values) or only affect the values materialize() produces, through BasicJsonType.

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• Only 64-bit integers. basic_json_document<BasicJsonType> requires BasicJsonType::number_integer_t and number_unsigned_t to both be 64 bits wide; this is a compile-time static_assert.
  • A 4 GiB input limit. An input of 4294967280 bytes (4 GiB minus 16 bytes) or more throws out_of_range.416, a limit basic_json::parse() does not have. It keeps an index entry at 16 bytes: offsets and counts are 32 bits wide. The limit is 16 bytes below 2^32, because the parser reads in 16-byte steps, and a position one step past the end must still fit.
  • A stream is always read to its end. There is no partial/streaming read of an std::istream: the stream is read to its end into a buffer the document owns, and parsing starts after that.
  • No source positions on materialize(). Even with JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS enabled, materialize() does not set them. The index has the start offset of every value, but not the end of arrays, objects, and escaped strings, which the positions also need.
  • Objects iterate in document order. begin()/ end() and items() visit an object's members in the order they appear in the source text. basic_json's default object_t is a std::map, which sorts by key, so iterating a materialize()d value can print members in a different order than iterating the view they came from.
  • Chained access is safe. operator[] with a missing key, an index out of range, or an unresolvable JSON pointer returns a discarded view, and operator[] on a discarded view returns a discarded view without throwing: v["a"]["b"][0] can be tested once at the end. Type errors on values that exist (a key on an array, an index on an object) still throw, and at throws for every missing value.
  • Duplicate keys: lookups find the first member, parse() keeps the last. See Duplicate keys below.
  • No JSON_DIAGNOSTICS path. Exceptions thrown by basic_json_view's own element access and lookup functions never carry the JSON Pointer path JSON_DIAGNOSTICS would otherwise add: the view has no basic_json value to point at, so the exception is created without one, regardless of how BasicJsonType was built.
  • Ordering comparisons are not provided by basic_json_view — there is no operator<. operator== and operator!= are provided, though: two views, or a view and a BasicJsonType value, compare equal exactly when materialize() or parse() would produce equal values for them, without ever building a tree to do it. For ordering, too, materialize() is the way to get a value you can compare.

docs.title: Duplicate keys
docs.text:
A lookup in a view and in the parsed value can give different answers

If an object in the source text repeats a key, operator[], at, find, value, contains, and JSON pointer resolution all return the first member with that key. basic_json::parse() instead keeps the last value of a repeated key, so for {"a":1,"a":2}, view["a"] is 1 while parse(text)["a"] is 2. count counts every member with the key, so it is 2 here.

begin()/end() and items() visit every occurrence, in document order, and size() counts all of them, so view.size() can be larger than view.materialize().size().

Why the first? A lookup can stop as soon as it finds a match. Returning the last member would force every lookup to scan all members of the object, even when the key is found at the very first one: this made lookups in small objects 1.6 to 3.4 times slower. The hash index of the keys of objects with 128 members or more leads to the first member of a key as well. Other zero-copy parsers that index the source text, such as yyjson and simdjson, also return the first member. RFC 8259 only says that names within an object SHOULD be unique and that the behavior of a receiver that sees duplicates is unpredictable, so neither choice is wrong.

The same holds for get<T>() of a type whose from_json() reads the view, such as the types of the NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_* macros: their members are looked up, so get<point>() of {"x":1,"x":2} reads x == 1, while materialize().get<point>() reads 2.

What stays the same as parse()? materialize() and get<std::map<...>>() replay every member in order, so they keep the last value exactly like basic_json::parse() (at the position of the first occurrence of the key, for an ordered_json).

How do I get the value parse() would give? Either call view.materialize() and look the key up in the result, or iterate the members and keep the last match:

// the last member with the key "a", as parse() would keep it
json_view last;
for (const auto item : view.items())
{
    if (item.key() == "a")
    {
        last = item.value();
    }
}

If you cannot trust the source text to have unique keys, check size() against the number of distinct keys, or reject duplicates when iterating.

docs.title: Getting values out without copying
docs.text:
get<T>() converts most T directly from the flat index, without ever building a basic_json value for the conversion: bool, arithmetic types, std::nullptr_t, std::string/other std::basic_strings (copied once), basic_json_view itself, the standard containers and other types the library converts (std::vector, std::map, std::list, std::array, std::pair, std::tuple, std::optional, ...), and the types of the NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_* and NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM macros. Types whose from_json() is written for basic_json only go through materialize().get<T>() instead: the subtree is built into a real basic_json value first, exactly as parse() would, and converted from there. See Writing generic code for how to write a from_json() that reads views.

Two conversions never copy at all:

  • get_string() (equivalently, get<string_view_t>()) returns a string as a string_view_t pointing into the document's source() text — or, for a string that contains escape sequences, into the document's own buffer of decoded strings — instead of allocating a new std::string.
  • number_token() returns a number exactly as it was written in the source, e.g. "1.50", "1E2", or an integer with more digits than any number type holds, instead of rounding it into a double/int64_t the way get<T>() (and basic_json::parse()) would.

Both results are only valid as long as the view — and, for a string with no escapes, the borrowed source text — is.

docs.title: Writing generic code
docs.text:
A view's type names its BasicJsonType and its view_mode: json_view is basic_json_view<json, view_mode::read_only>, and json_editable_view is basic_json_view<json, view_mode::editable>. These are different types. The only conversion between them turns a view of a read-only document into a view of an editable document of the same BasicJsonType, so a function written for one shortcut accepts few other views:

void print_names(json_view v);           // accepts neither an ordered_json_view nor a json_editable_view
void print_names(json_editable_view v);  // also accepts a json_view, but no ordered_json_view

This is the same pitfall as a to_json/from_json written for json instead of any BasicJsonType, which then does not work for ordered_json. The shortcuts are for declaring documents and views; a function that takes a view names the views it accepts with a template:

// views of editable documents only
template<typename BasicJsonType>
void f(basic_json_view<BasicJsonType, view_mode::editable> v);

// views of read-only documents only
template<typename BasicJsonType>
void f(basic_json_view<BasicJsonType, view_mode::read_only> v);

// views of either document type
template<typename BasicJsonType, view_mode Mode>
void f(basic_json_view<BasicJsonType, Mode> v);

Views are passed by value: they are two pointers, cheap to copy, like a std::string_view. A const& works as well, but a non-const reference does not bind to the views that root(), operator[], and at() return, so f(doc.root()) would not compile.

There is no conversion from an editable view to a read-only one, by design: the mode decides how a view walks the index. A read-only view reads a container in place, while a view of an editable document follows the links that edits leave behind, so a read-only view of an edited document would read stale values. The other direction is safe: a read-only document has no edits, so a view of it converts to an editable view, which reads it like an editable document before its first edit. A template deduces the mode without conversions, so the template forms above still accept only the modes they name. Views of both modes compare with operator==.

is_json_view<T> tells views from other types, for constraints that cannot be written as a basic_json_view<...> parameter.

docs.title: A from_json() that reads views
docs.text:
get<T>() on a view calls T's from_json() with the view itself if that from_json() accepts views, and with materialize() otherwise. The from_json() functions of the NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_*, NLOHMANN_DEFINE_DERIVED_TYPE_*, and NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM macros, and those of the library for the standard types, accept views, so these types need nothing else. For decoding the statuses of twitter.json into structs, reading the view is about 5 times faster than materialize().get<T>().

A hand-written from_json() reads views if it is constrained to json values and views:

template < typename J, typename std::enable_if <
               nlohmann::is_json_view<J>::value || std::is_same<J, nlohmann::json>::value, int >::type = 0 >
void from_json(const J& j, person& p)
{
    p.name = j.at("name").template get<std::string>();
    p.age = j.at("age").template get<int>();
}

Its body may only use what views and basic_json have in common: the type checks, at(), operator[], contains(), value(), size(), iteration and items(), and get<T>()/get_to(). An unconstrained template<typename BasicJsonType> void from_json(const BasicJsonType& j, person& p), as in arbitrary type conversions, is never called with a view, as it might use basic_json functions a view does not have; such a type is converted through materialize(). A from_json() for json only is converted through materialize() as well.

Two things differ when a from_json() reads the view:

  • Duplicate keys. Members looked up by name (at(), value(), ... and thus the macros) find the first member with a repeated key, see Duplicate keys; materialize().get<T>() would see the last one. Containers built from an object, such as std::map, keep the last value either way, as parse() does.
  • JSON_DIAGNOSTICS. Exceptions thrown by the view carry no path to the value.

to_json() is unaffected: it writes basic_json values, never views.

docs.title: Writing a view back
docs.text:
dump() serializes a view directly from the flat index, without ever building a basic_json value. An object's members are written in document order, not sorted by key, and every occurrence of a repeated key is written, not only the last one — the same two ways iteration already differs from a materialize()d value, see Duplicate keys. materialize().dump() gives a different result in both respects for a json_view.

By default, numbers are written the way basic_json::dump() would. number_format::source instead copies every number exactly as it was written in the source text — a price like 19.90, a long order or account ID with more digits than any number type holds, or a high-precision coordinate — something basic_json cannot do at all, since parsing already reduces a number to its parsed double/int64_t value.

operator<< writes a view to a stream the way basic_json's does, using the stream's width/fill for indentation.

docs.title: Editing a document
docs.text:
Everything above is read-only: a json_document/json_view lets you look at a parsed text without copying it, but not change it. basic_json_document<BasicJsonType, view_mode::editable> — more conveniently spelled json_editable_document or ordered_json_editable_document — also lets you set a value, push_back onto or insert into an array, and erase an object member or an array element, still without ever building a basic_json tree for parts you do not touch.

The mode defaults to view_mode::read_only, so json_document/ordered_json_document are unaffected — they carry none of the bookkeeping edits need, and calling set/push_back/insert/erase on one is a compile error, not a runtime one.

docs.title: Why: editing without reformatting
docs.text:
The 19.90 price from above is exactly the kind of value that makes editing a json or ordered_json value in place lossy. Say you parse a configuration file, patch one field, and write it back:

  • json re-sorts every key on the way in (object_t is a std::map) and rewrites every number to its shortest round-trip form on the way out — a one-field patch turns into a diff that reorders the whole file and rewrites 19.90 to 19.9.
  • ordered_json keeps the key order, but still rewrites every number the same way: parsing has already reduced it to a double/int64_t, and there is no way back to how it was spelled in the source text.

The patch of the example below (set "host", add "retries") written back by each of them:

json

keys sorted, numbers rewritten

{"host":"db2",
 "name":"cache",
 "port":6379,
 "price":19.9,
 "retries":3}

ordered_json

key order kept, numbers rewritten

{"name":"cache",
 "host":"db2",
 "port":6379,
 "price":19.9,
 "retries":3}

json_editable_document

order and spelling kept

{"name":"cache",
 "host":"db2",
 "port":6379,
 "price":19.90,
 "retries":3}

An editable document keeps both. dump() of an edited document writes members in document order — a member set added goes at the end, exactly where it was inserted, and an erased member simply leaves a gap: everything around it keeps its place — and number_format::source keeps the exact spelling of every number an edit did not itself touch; a number an edit did touch is written the way BasicJsonType::dump() would write it, since there is no source spelling for a brand new value.

Example: patch a configuration, keeping member order and number spellings 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;
using nlohmann::json_editable_document;
using nlohmann::json_editable_view;

int main()
{
    // a configuration file, as it might be read from disk
    const std::string text = R"({"name": "cache", "host": "db1", "port": 6379, "price": 19.90})";
    std::cout << text << "\n\n";

    // patch two fields -- "price" is never touched
    json_editable_document doc = json_editable_document::parse(text);
    doc.set(doc.root(), "host", "db2");
    doc.set(doc.root(), "retries", 3);

    // member order (the new member at the end) and the untouched number's
    // exact spelling survive
    std::cout << doc.root().dump(-1, ' ', false, json_editable_view::number_format::source) << '\n';

    // the same patch on a plain json value: keys are sorted (object_t is a
    // std::map), and "price" is rewritten even though the patch never
    // touched it
    json plain = json::parse(text);
    plain["host"] = "db2";
    plain["retries"] = 3;
    std::cout << plain.dump() << '\n';
}

Output:

{"name": "cache", "host": "db1", "port": 6379, "price": 19.90}

{"name":"cache","host":"db2","port":6379,"price":19.90,"retries":3}
{"host":"db2","name":"cache","port":6379,"price":19.9,"retries":3}

docs.title: What stays valid, and what an edit costs
docs.text:
The source text itself is never written, and the parsed index never moves — a value keeps the node it was parsed into for as long as it is not itself replaced. So every view taken before an edit, including a previously obtained root(), stays valid and, if it still refers to the edited value, sees the edit; a view of a value a later edit drops or replaces just keeps showing what it last held. New values go to storage the document allocates and owns on demand. The one thing an edit does invalidate is the iterators taken over an edited array or object: the first time an element is added to it, inserted into it, erased from it, or replaced by a value that spans a different number of nodes, its elements move from the parsed, fixed layout to a growable block of links so that push_back can later grow it in amortized constant time — existing elements are not touched, but an iterator that was walking the old layout no longer matches. A string obtained with get_string() is unaffected either way and stays valid across further edits. See basic_json_document's Edits for the details, and set's Exception safety for what an edit guarantees if it throws (the basic guarantee, not the strong one dump() and the read-only functions provide). How edits are kept in the index is described in the architecture overview.

Step through the edits of a small document (the node fields follow the architecture overview):

Step 1 of 5: parsed After parse: nine nodes, nothing owned yet. The dump with number_format::source is {"port":6379,"price":19.90,"tags":["eu","a\"b"]}. parsed index: fixed, never moves the source text is never written 0 object { } 3 1 key port 2 uint 6379 3 key price 4 float 19.90 5 key tags 6 array [ ] 2 7 string "eu" 8 string a"b owned storage: allocated on demand, never moves empty: a read-only json_document has none of this view v = root()["tags"] (taken after parse): valid, sees every edit iterator over tags (taken after parse): valid dump(): {"port":6379,"price":19.90,"tags":["eu","a\"b"]} Step 1 of 5. After parsing: nine nodes in the parsed index, no owned storage yet. Step 2 of 5: doc.set(doc.root(), "port", 6380) set: the node of the integer is overwritten in place. The dump with number_format::source is {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["eu","a\"b"]}. parsed index: fixed, never moves the source text is never written 0 object { } 3 1 key port 2 uint 6380 3 key price 4 float 19.90 5 key tags 6 array [ ] 2 7 string "eu" 8 string a"b owned storage: allocated on demand, never moves empty: a read-only json_document has none of this view v = root()["tags"] (taken after parse): valid, sees every edit iterator over tags (taken after parse): valid dump(): {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["eu","a\"b"]} Step 2 of 5. doc.set(doc.root(), "port", 6380) overwrites the node of the integer in place; no member is added or removed, so the object keeps its parsed layout. Step 3 of 5: doc.erase(doc.root()["tags"], 0) erase: the array moves to a block of links in owned storage. The dump with number_format::source is {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b"]}. parsed index: fixed, never moves the source text is never written 0 object { } 3 1 key port 2 uint 6380 3 key price 4 float 19.90 5 key tags 6 array moved [ ] 2 7 string "eu" unreferenced 8 string a"b owned storage: allocated on demand, never moves 0' header [ ] 1 1' link → 8 free view v = root()["tags"] (taken after parse): valid, sees every edit iterator over tags (taken after parse): invalid: tags no longer uses the parsed layout dump(): {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b"]} Step 3 of 5. doc.erase(doc.root()["tags"], 0): the array is edited for the first time, so its elements move to a block of links in owned storage. The node of "eu" stays in the index, but nothing refers to it any more; iterators over the array taken before are invalid. Step 4 of 5: doc.push_back(doc.root()["tags"], "new") push_back: a new node, and a link appended to the block. The dump with number_format::source is {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b","new"]}. parsed index: fixed, never moves the source text is never written 0 object { } 3 1 key port 2 uint 6380 3 key price 4 float 19.90 5 key tags 6 array moved [ ] 2 7 string "eu" unreferenced 8 string a"b owned storage: allocated on demand, never moves 0' header [ ] 2 1' link → 8 2' link → 3' 3' string "new" edited text new view v = root()["tags"] (taken after parse): valid, sees every edit iterator over tags (taken after parse): invalid: tags no longer uses the parsed layout dump(): {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b","new"]} Step 4 of 5. doc.push_back(doc.root()["tags"], "new"): the new string gets its own node, its text goes to the buffer of edited text, and a link to it is appended to the block of the array. Step 5 of 5: doc.set(doc.root(), "retries", 3) set of a new member: the object moves to a block as well. The dump with number_format::source is {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b","new"],"retries":3}. parsed index: fixed, never moves the source text is never written 0 object moved { } 3 1 key port 2 uint 6380 3 key price 4 float 19.90 5 key tags 6 array moved [ ] 2 7 string "eu" unreferenced 8 string a"b owned storage: allocated on demand, never moves 0' header [ ] 2 1' link → 8 2' link → 3' 3' string "new" 4' uint 3 5' header { } 4 6' key port 7' link → 2 8' key price 9' link → 4 10' key tags 11' link → 6 12' key retries 13' link → 4' edited text newretries view v = root()["tags"] (taken after parse): valid, sees every edit iterator over tags (taken after parse): invalid: tags no longer uses the parsed layout dump(): {"port":6380,"price":19.90,"tags":["a\"b","new"],"retries":3} Step 5 of 5. doc.set(doc.root(), "retries", 3): a new member, so the object moves to a block too: copies of its keys, links to the values it already had, then the new key and a link to the new integer.

The node index and the owned storage of the document after each of five edits. Use Back, Next, or the numbered buttons to switch between the steps; without JavaScript all steps are shown one below the other.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
save() writes a document as an image: a byte buffer that load() reads back into a document without parsing — no lexing, no building the node index, nothing but copying the nodes and pointing the text and the decoded strings at the image. Where parse_copy() still has to scan the whole input, load() turns that scan into a copy of the node index alone.

Why. A document that is parsed once and then read many times — a configuration loaded at startup, a template rendered on every request, a large reference dataset a worker process needs in memory — pays for parsing once but can amortize save()'s cost across every later load. That makes images useful for a cache: save a document the first time it is parsed (to a file, a shared-memory segment, an in-process cache), and load() it on every later use instead of parsing the source text again. They are just as useful for handing a parsed document to another process (or a forked worker) running the same build of the library, since load() turns the transfer into a copy of the node index plus pointers into the received bytes, not a re-parse.

Choosing a check. load() takes an image_check that trades validation against speed: image_check::full (the default) checks everything the parser itself guarantees, so a checked image is exactly as safe to read and serialize as a freshly parsed document — the right choice whenever the image did not come straight from this process's own save(), such as a file or a network peer. image_check::bounds only checks structure and bounds — cheaper, since it skips scanning the text and the decoded strings — and fits a cache the process trusts, one it wrote and reads back itself. image_check::none skips validation entirely, for an image trusted as much as the process's own memory. See load()'s Notes for exactly what each level does and does not guarantee.

Example: cache a parsed configuration as an image 
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

using nlohmann::json_document;

int main()
{
    std::cout << std::boolalpha;

    // a configuration a service parses once and then caches as an image, so
    // that later requests can load() it instead of parsing the text again
    const std::string text = R"({"name": "cache", "host": "db1", "port": 6379, "replicas": ["db2", "db3"]})";
    const json_document config = json_document::parse(text);

    // save() turns the parsed document into a byte buffer: a 64-byte header,
    // the node index, the source text, and the decoded strings
    const std::vector<std::uint8_t> image = config.save();
    std::cout << image.size() << '\n';

    // the same document always saves to the same bytes
    std::cout << (image == json_document::parse(text).save()) << '\n';

    // loading the image back needs no parsing, yet dumps exactly what
    // parsing the text produced
    const json_document reloaded = json_document::load(image);
    std::cout << (reloaded.root().dump() == config.root().dump()) << '\n';
}

Output:

316
true
true

Experimental

The image format is versioned but not yet stable, and may change in an incompatible way before it is declared stable. It is little-endian only (on big-endian targets, save() and load() do not exist), and tied to the library build that wrote it — use it to cache a document or to hand one to another process running the same build, not as a long-term storage format; keep the original JSON text if a saved document needs to be readable by a future library version.

The idea of a document you can read without parsing comes from zero-copy formats such as FlatBuffers and YaFF; the check load() runs follows the idea of FlatBuffers' Verifier. No code is taken from either.

docs.title: Choosing between json, ordered_json, the SAX interface, and json_view
docs.text:
json / ordered_json SAX interface json_document / json_view json_editable_document / json_editable_view Ownership owns every value owns nothing; you decide what to keep, in your handler borrows or owns the text; the index is always owned by the document same as json_document; edits go to storage the document owns Mutability freely mutable not applicable (a one-shot event stream) read-only set/push_back/insert/erase edit in place; the source text is never rewritten What you get a full tree you can read, write, and keep as long as you like a sequence of callbacks; whatever your handler builds from them a flat index plus, on demand, materialize()d json/ordered_json values for the parts you actually use the same, plus dump() of an edited document that keeps the member order and, with number_format::source, the spelling of every untouched number Typical use general-purpose JSON handling: config, request/response bodies you build or modify, anything you hold onto validating or projecting a text into your own data structure without ever holding the whole thing as JSON large or high-volume input where you only need part of it, or need it repeatedly, and can keep the source text (or a copy) alive for as long as the document lives a document you read, patch a few fields of, and write back — a configuration file, for instance — where the rest of it should come back exactly as it was Caching/reload not applicable — re-parse, or roll your own serialization not applicable save()/load(): cache the parsed index as an image and reload it without parsing same, saving the document's current — possibly edited — state

Each column is one way to work with JSON in this library, and each row compares one property of them.

docs.title: Supported Macros
docs.text: Some aspects of the library can be configured by defining preprocessor macros before including the json.hpp header. See also the API documentation for macros for examples and more information.

docs.title: JSON_ASSERT(x)
docs.text:
This macro controls which code is executed for runtime assertions of the library.

See full documentation of JSON_ASSERT(x).

docs.title: JSON_BRACE_INIT_COPY_SEMANTICS
docs.text:
When defined to 1, single-element brace initialization of a basic_json value (e.g., json j{value};) is treated as a copy/move of the element rather than wrapping it in a single-element array. The default value is 0, which preserves the existing behavior.

See full documentation of JSON_BRACE_INIT_COPY_SEMANTICS.

docs.text:
This macro overrides catch calls inside the library.

See full documentation of JSON_CATCH_USER(exception).

docs.title: JSON_DELETE_DEPRECATED_FUNCTIONS
docs.text:
When defined to 1, all deprecated functions are declared as deleted instead of only being marked as deprecated, so code that still calls them no longer compiles. This way, you can find all calls that need to be replaced before version 4.0.0 removes these functions.

The macro can also be set with the CMake option JSON_DeleteDeprecatedFunctions (OFF by default).

See full documentation of JSON_DELETE_DEPRECATED_FUNCTIONS.

docs.title: JSON_DIAGNOSTICS
docs.text:
This macro enables extended diagnostics for exception messages. Possible values are 1 to enable or 0 to disable (default).

When enabled, exception messages contain a JSON Pointer to the JSON value that triggered the exception, see Extended diagnostic messages for an example. Note that enabling this macro increases the size of every JSON value by one pointer and adds some runtime overhead.

The diagnostics messages can also be controlled with the CMake option JSON_Diagnostics (OFF by default) which sets JSON_DIAGNOSTICS accordingly.

See full documentation of JSON_DIAGNOSTICS.

docs.title: JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS
docs.text:
When enabled, two new member functions start_pos() and end_pos() are added to basic_json values. If the value was created by calling theparse function, then these functions allow querying the byte positions of the value in the input it was parsed from. The byte positions are also used in exceptions to help locate errors.

The diagnostics positions can also be controlled with the CMake option JSON_Diagnostic_Positions (OFF by default) which sets JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS accordingly.

See full documentation of JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS

docs.title: JSON_HAS_CPP_11, JSON_HAS_CPP_14, JSON_HAS_CPP_17, JSON_HAS_CPP_20, JSON_HAS_CPP_23, JSON_HAS_CPP_26
docs.text:
The library targets C++11, but also supports some features introduced in later C++ versions (e.g., std::string_view support for C++17). For these new features, the library implements some preprocessor checks to determine the C++ standard. By defining any of these symbols, the internal check is overridden and the provided C++ version is unconditionally assumed. This can be helpful for compilers that only implement parts of the standard and would be detected incorrectly.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_CPP_11, JSON_HAS_CPP_14, JSON_HAS_CPP_17, JSON_HAS_CPP_20, JSON_HAS_CPP_23, and JSON_HAS_CPP_26.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM, JSON_HAS_EXPERIMENTAL_FILESYSTEM
docs.text:
When compiling with C++17, the library provides conversions from and to std::filesystem::path. As compiler support for filesystem is limited, the library tries to detect whether <filesystem>/std::filesystem (JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM) or <experimental/filesystem>/std::experimental::filesystem (JSON_HAS_EXPERIMENTAL_FILESYSTEM) should be used. To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM or JSON_HAS_EXPERIMENTAL_FILESYSTEM to 1.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM and JSON_HAS_EXPERIMENTAL_FILESYSTEM.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_RANGES
docs.text:
The library uses std::ranges (and concepts) where available, for example, to parse from C++20 ranges and to construct JSON arrays from range views. The library detects whether the standard library supports ranges and disables the support on toolchains with an incomplete implementation. To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_RANGES to 1 or 0.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_RANGES.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_RANGE_VIEW_CONVERSION
docs.text:
When JSON_HAS_RANGES is enabled (and the compiler is not MinGW), a JSON array can be constructed directly from a C++20 range view such as std::views::filter(...). To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_RANGE_VIEW_CONVERSION to 1 or 0.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_RANGE_VIEW_CONVERSION.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_STATIC_RTTI
docs.text:
The library detects whether the compiler supports run time type information (RTTI), which it needs, for instance, to exclude std::any from the candidate types of the implicit conversion on C++17. To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_STATIC_RTTI to 1 or 0.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_STATIC_RTTI.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_STD_FORMAT
docs.text:
When compiling with C++20 and a standard library that provides <format>, the library provides a std::formatter specialization for JSON values. To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_STD_FORMAT to 1 or 0.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_STD_FORMAT.

docs.title: JSON_HAS_THREE_WAY_COMPARISON
docs.text:
When the compiler and standard library support 3-way comparison (the spaceship operator <=>), the library provides it for JSON values. To override the built-in check, define JSON_HAS_THREE_WAY_COMPARISON to 1 or 0.

See full documentation of JSON_HAS_THREE_WAY_COMPARISON.

docs.title: JSON_NOEXCEPTION
docs.text:
Exceptions can be switched off by defining the symbol JSON_NOEXCEPTION.

See full documentation of JSON_NOEXCEPTION.

docs.title: JSON_DISABLE_ENUM_SERIALIZATION
docs.text:
When defined, default parse and serialize functions for enums are excluded and have to be provided by the user, for example, using NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM.

See full documentation of JSON_DISABLE_ENUM_SERIALIZATION.

docs.title: JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN
docs.text:
When defined to 1, parsing from a std::istream reads one character at a time instead of scanning the characters that the stream buffer holds in bulk. Results are the same either way; the macro is an escape hatch for stream buffers that do not follow the usual std::streambuf contract. The default value is 0.

See full documentation of JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN.

docs.title: JSON_DISABLE_TUPLE_REFERENCE_CONVERSION
docs.text:
When defined to 1, a JSON value can no longer be created from a one-element std::tuple holding a reference to a JSON value, such as the result of std::forward_as_tuple(j). This lets std::tuple convert such tuples element-wise. This is planned to become the default in version 4.0.0.

See full documentation of JSON_DISABLE_TUPLE_REFERENCE_CONVERSION.

docs.title: JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO
docs.text:
When defined to 1, parsing from a FILE* reads every character with std::fgetc, which locks the file each time, instead of locking the file once and reading it with the unlocked stdio functions. Results are the same either way. The default value is 0.

See full documentation of JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO.

docs.title: JSON_NO_AUTOMATIC_UDLS
docs.text:
When defined, <nlohmann/json.hpp> does not include <nlohmann/json_literals.hpp> with the user-defined string literals operator""_json and operator""_json_pointer. This reduces the compile time of translation units that do not use them, because the literals instantiate the parser in every translation unit that includes them. Include <nlohmann/json_literals.hpp> where the literals are needed.

See full documentation of JSON_NO_AUTOMATIC_UDLS.

docs.title: JSON_NO_IO
docs.text:
When defined, headers <cstdio>, <ios>, <iosfwd>, <istream>, and <ostream> are not included and parse functions relying on these headers are excluded. This is relevant for environment where these I/O functions are disallowed for security reasons (e.g., Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX)).

See full documentation of JSON_NO_IO.

docs.title: JSON_NO_SIMD
docs.text:
When defined, the library uses only portable code instead of vector instructions (SSE2, SSSE3, NEON) for scanning strings and writing floating-point numbers. Results are the same either way. It is not defined by default.

See full documentation of JSON_NO_SIMD.

docs.title: JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL
docs.text:
When defined, the library does not use thread_local storage. Copying a value and comparing two values then always avoid the call stack rather than descending into a bounded number of levels first, which is slower but yields the same values and the same comparisons.

See full documentation of JSON_NO_THREAD_LOCAL.

docs.title: JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION
docs.text:
When defined to 1, operator>> and non-strict sax_parse leave an input stream positioned right after the parsed value, instead of also consuming the character that terminates a number. The default value is 0, which preserves the existing behavior; this is planned to become the default in version 4.0.0.

See full documentation of JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION.

docs.title: JSON_SKIP_LIBRARY_VERSION_CHECK
docs.text:
When defined, the library will not create a compiler warning when a different version of the library was already included.

See full documentation of JSON_SKIP_LIBRARY_VERSION_CHECK.

docs.title: JSON_SKIP_UNSUPPORTED_COMPILER_CHECK
docs.text:
When defined, the library will not create a compile error when a known unsupported compiler is detected. This allows using the library with compilers that do not fully support C++11 and may only work if unsupported features are not used.

See full documentation of JSON_SKIP_UNSUPPORTED_COMPILER_CHECK.

docs.title: JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8
docs.text:
When defined to 1, to_cbor, to_ubjson, to_bjdata, and to_bson throw type_error.316 for a string value or object key that is not valid UTF-8. The default value is 0, which writes the bytes unchanged as before version 3.13.0 unreleased; this is planned to become the default in version 4.0.0.

The check can also be enabled with the CMake option JSON_StrictBinaryUTF8 (OFF by default) which sets JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8 accordingly.

See full documentation of JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8.

docs.title: JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING
docs.text:
When defined to 1, a '\0' (NUL) byte anywhere in the input is rejected with parse_error.101, like any other unexpected byte, instead of being silently treated as end of input (see the FAQ entry for background). The default value is 0, which preserves the existing behavior; this is planned to become the default in version 4.0.0.

The strict handling can also be enabled with the CMake option JSON_StrictNulHandling (OFF by default) which sets JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING accordingly.

See full documentation of JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING.

docs.title: JSON_THROW_USER(exception)
docs.text:
This macro overrides throw calls inside the library. The argument is the exception to be thrown.

See full documentation of JSON_THROW_USER(exception).

docs.title: JSON_TRY_USER
docs.text:
This macro overrides try calls inside the library.

See full documentation of JSON_TRY_USER.

docs.title: JSON_USE_IMPLICIT_CONVERSIONS
docs.text:
When defined to 0, implicit conversions are switched off. By default, implicit conversions are switched on.

See full documentation of JSON_USE_IMPLICIT_CONVERSIONS.

docs.title: JSON_USE_GLOBAL_UDLS
docs.text:
When defined to 1 (default), the user-defined string literals operator""_json and operator""_json_pointer are placed into the global namespace instead of nlohmann::literals::json_literals.

See full documentation of JSON_USE_GLOBAL_UDLS.

docs.title: JSON_USE_LEGACY_DISCARDED_VALUE_COMPARISON
docs.text:
When defined to 1, the library restores the legacy behavior in which comparing a discarded value with <= or >= yields true instead of false. This behavior is deprecated and switched off (0) by default.

See full documentation of JSON_USE_LEGACY_DISCARDED_VALUE_COMPARISON.

docs.title: JSON_USE_OBJECTS_FOR_ENUM_KEYED_MAPS
docs.text:
When defined to 1, maps with enum keys (e.g., std::map<E, T>) are stored as objects, using the enum's conversion for the keys, instead of arrays of [key, value] pairs. It is switched off (0) by default.

See full documentation of JSON_USE_OBJECTS_FOR_ENUM_KEYED_MAPS.

docs.title: JSON_USE_SIMDUTF
docs.text:
When defined, UTF-8 validation of JSON strings read from contiguous byte input is delegated to the simdutf library instead of the built-in scalar validator. This is an opt-in external dependency and is not defined by default.

See full documentation of JSON_USE_SIMDUTF.

docs.title: NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_*(...), NLOHMANN_DEFINE_DERIVED_TYPE_*(...)
docs.text: The library defines 12 macros to simplify the serialization/deserialization of types. See the page on arbitrary type conversion for a detailed discussion.

docs.title: NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE, NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_BEGIN, NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_END, NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_NO_VERSION
docs.text:
These macros relate to the versioned, inline nlohmann namespace:

  • NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE evaluates to the full name of the nlohmann namespace (including the inline ABI namespace).
  • NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_BEGIN / NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_END open and close the namespace (for example, to add specializations).
  • NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_NO_VERSION, when defined to 1, omits the version component from the inline namespace.

See the nlohmann Namespace page, and the full documentation of NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE, NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_BEGIN / NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_END, and NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_NO_VERSION.

docs.title: NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM(type, ...)
docs.text:
This macro simplifies the serialization/deserialization of enum types. See Specializing enum conversion for more information.

See full documentation of NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM.

A strict variant NLOHMANN_JSON_SERIALIZE_ENUM_STRICT throws an exception on undefined input instead of falling back to the first mapping.

docs.title: NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_MAJOR, NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_MINOR, NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_PATCH
docs.text:
These macros are defined by the library and contain the version numbers according to Semantic Versioning 2.0.0.

See full documentation of NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_MAJOR, NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_MINOR, and NLOHMANN_JSON_VERSION_PATCH.

  • Modules - macros and C++20 modules

docs.title: JSON Merge Patch
docs.text:
The library supports JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) as a patch format. The merge patch format is primarily intended for use with the HTTP PATCH method as a means of describing a set of modifications to a target resource's content. Applying a merge patch changes the JSON value the patch is applied to.

Instead of using JSON Pointer to specify values to be manipulated, it describes the changes using a syntax that closely mimics the document being modified. Unlike JSON Patch, a JSON Merge Patch cannot express every kind of change (e.g., it cannot reorder array elements or remove a specific array element), but it is easier to read and write for object-shaped documents.

The function merge_diff creates a merge patch that changes one JSON value into another.

The example below applies one patch to one document. Here is the document before:

{
    "title": "Goodbye!",
    "author": {
        "givenName": "John",
        "familyName": "Doe"
    },
    "tags": ["example", "sample"],
    "content": "This will be unchanged"
}

This is the patch:

{
    "title": "Hello!",
    "phoneNumber": "+01-123-456-7890",
    "author": {
        "familyName": null
    },
    "tags": ["example"]
}

And this is the document after applying it:

{
    "title": "Hello!",
    "author": {
        "givenName": "John"
    },
    "tags": ["example"],
    "content": "This will be unchanged",
    "phoneNumber": "+01-123-456-7890"
}

The table goes through the members one by one. "Member" is the name of an object member in the patch (and in the document); it is not a JSON Pointer and nothing of it is passed to the function: the whole patch is passed to merge_patch.

Rule Member Before Patch After change value title "Goodbye!" "Hello!" "Hello!" add key phoneNumber (no member) "+01-123-456-7890" "+01-123-456-7890" object merges recursively author {"givenName": "John", "familyName": "Doe"} {"familyName": null} {"givenName": "John"} null removes key familyName inside author "Doe" null (removed) array replaced whole tags ["example", "sample"] ["example"] ["example"] unchanged key content "This will be unchanged" (no member) "This will be unchanged"

An array in the patch replaces the array in the target, so a merge patch cannot change a single element. Each member of the patch is applied like this; a patch that is not an object replaces the whole target.

flowchart LR
    M["member of the patch"] --> N{{"value null?"}}
    N -->|yes| D["delete the key"]
    N -->|no| O{{"value an object?"}}
    O -->|yes| R["merge recursively into the target's value"]
    O -->|no| S["set the key to the value"]

How one member of a merge patch is applied: a null value deletes the key, an object is merged recursively, and any other value replaces the value of the key.

Not a general deep merge

A merge patch is not a general deep merge: a null value in the patch deletes the key from the target. To merge two objects recursively (e.g., defaults and user settings), use update with merge_objects set to true; see Merging objects.

Limitations of RFC 7396

  • A patch cannot set a member to null, because null removes the member: {"a":1} patched with {"a":null} gives {}.
  • Arrays are replaced as a whole, never merged, and a null inside an array is kept.
  • null members of the target that the patch does not mention are preserved.
  • A null that would remove a member of a not yet existing object still creates that object: {} patched with {"a":{"b":null}} gives {"a":{}}.
  • A patch that is not an object replaces the whole target (a null patch makes the target null); an object patch applied to a non-object target starts from an empty object.
  • merge_diff has a matching limitation for null members.
Example

The following code shows how a JSON Merge Patch is applied to a JSON document.

#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>
#include <iomanip> // for std::setw

using nlohmann::json;
using namespace nlohmann::literals;

int main()
{
    // the original document
    json document = R"({
                "title": "Goodbye!",
                "author": {
                    "givenName": "John",
                    "familyName": "Doe"
                },
                "tags": [
                    "example",
                    "sample"
                ],
                "content": "This will be unchanged"
            })"_json;

    // the patch
    json patch = R"({
                "title": "Hello!",
                "phoneNumber": "+01-123-456-7890",
                "author": {
                    "familyName": null
                },
                "tags": [
                    "example"
                ]
            })"_json;

    // apply the patch
    document.merge_patch(patch);

    // output original and patched document
    std::cout << std::setw(4) << document << '\n';
}

Output:

{
    "author": {
        "givenName": "John"
    },
    "content": "This will be unchanged",
    "phoneNumber": "+01-123-456-7890",
    "tags": [
        "example"
    ],
    "title": "Hello!"
}

docs.title: Modifying values
docs.text: Once a JSON value exists, its content can be changed: elements can be added, replaced, merged, and removed. This page gives an overview of the available operations. For read access, see element access.

docs.title: Adding to arrays
docs.text:
New elements are appended to an array with push_back or constructed in place with emplace_back. If the value is null, it is converted to an array first, so these functions can also be used to build an array from scratch.

json j;                 // null
j.push_back(1);         // [1]
j.push_back(2);         // [1,2]
j.emplace_back(3);      // [1,2,3]

// operator+= is a shorthand for push_back
j += 4;                 // [1,2,3,4]

docs.title: Adding to objects
docs.text:
The most common way to add or replace a member is operator[], which inserts the key if it does not exist yet:

json j;
j["name"] = "Mary";     // {"name":"Mary"}
j["name"] = "John";     // {"name":"John"}  (replaced)

emplace inserts a member only if the key is not already present, and reports whether the insertion happened — useful for "add if absent" semantics.

docs.title: Merging objects
docs.text:
To merge one object into another, update copies all members from another object (similar to Python's dict.update). This is the idiomatic way to combine two objects. It has two modes:

  • By default, the merge is shallow: existing keys are overwritten, even if both values are objects.
  • With merge_objects = #!cpp true, keys whose values are objects in both JSON values are merged recursively. Everything else is overwritten. In particular, arrays are replaced, not concatenated.
Example 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;
using namespace nlohmann::literals;

int main()
{
    // create two JSON objects
    json o1 = R"( {"color": "red", "price": 17.99, "names": {"de": "Flugzeug"}} )"_json;
    json o2 = R"( {"color": "blue", "speed": 100, "names": {"en": "plane"}} )"_json;
    json o3 = o1;

    // add all keys from o2 to o1 (updating "color", replacing "names")
    o1.update(o2);

    // add all keys from o2 to o1 (updating "color", merging "names")
    o3.update(o2, true);

    // output updated object o1 and o3
    std::cout << std::setw(2) << o1 << '\n';
    std::cout << std::setw(2) << o3 << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "color": "blue",
  "names": {
    "en": "plane"
  },
  "price": 17.99,
  "speed": 100
}
{
  "color": "blue",
  "names": {
    "de": "Flugzeug",
    "en": "plane"
  },
  "price": 17.99,
  "speed": 100
}

A common use of the recursive mode is combining defaults with user settings. Nested defaults that the user did not set are kept:

json defaults = {{"log", {{"level", "info"}, {"file", "app.log"}}}, {"retries", 3}};
json user_settings = {{"log", {{"level", "debug"}}}};

json config = defaults;
config.update(user_settings, true);
// {"log":{"file":"app.log","level":"debug"},"retries":3}

JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) also merges objects recursively, but it is a different tool: a null in the patch means "remove this key". It is meant for applying merge patch documents (e.g., received via HTTP PATCH). To merge configuration-like objects, use update(..., true). To apply a sequence of well-defined edit operations, see JSON Patch.

docs.title: Removing elements
docs.text:
Elements are removed with erase, which accepts an object key, an array index, or an iterator. clear empties a value while keeping its type, and operator[] combined with assignment can overwrite a value entirely.

json j = {{"a", 1}, {"b", 2}, {"c", 3}};
j.erase("b");           // {"a":1,"c":3}

json a = {1, 2, 3, 4};
a.erase(1);             // [1,3,4]  (erase by index)

docs.title: Editing a document
docs.text: The operations above work on a basic_json value. A JSON text that was parsed into a document can also be changed in place, without building a basic_json tree for the parts that are not touched: set replaces a value, adds or replaces an object member, or replaces an array element (also through a JSON pointer), push_back appends to an array, insert inserts into an array (unlike basic_json::insert, it has no object overload; members are added with set), and erase removes a member or an element. These functions are available on the editable document types, such as json_editable_document.

  • merge_patch - apply an RFC 7396 merge patch
  • erase - / clear - remove elements

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
This library has experimental support for C++ modules, introduced in C++20. The library can be imported by writing import nlohmann.json; instead of #include <nlohmann/json.hpp>.

Please be aware that the module is experimental and a full test is outstanding, and the exported symbols are subject to change.

Importing the module instead of including the header reduces the compile time of every translation unit that uses the library, at the price of building the module once. The Compile times page has measurements and the one-off cost.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The nlohmann.json module requires that the build system is configured to build and resolve modules when imported. Obviously, as modules were introduced in C++20, this feature can only be used in C++20 and subsequent versions.

To enable building the nlohmann.json module (which is not done by default), the macro NLOHMANN_JSON_BUILD_MODULES must be passed to the build system.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
When using modules rather than headers, the previous example for creating a json object through a JSON file, would instead be: 

import std;
import nlohmann.json;

using nlohmann::json;

// ...

std::ifstream f("example.json");
json data = json::parse(f);

docs.title: Modules do not export macros
docs.text: It should be noted that as modules do not export macros, the nlohmann.json module will not export any macros.

docs.title: Exported symbols
docs.text:
Only the following symbols are exported from nlohmann.json:

  • nlohmann::adl_serializer
  • nlohmann::basic_json
  • nlohmann::basic_json_document
  • nlohmann::basic_json_view
  • nlohmann::json
  • nlohmann::json_document
  • nlohmann::json_pointer
  • nlohmann::json_view
  • nlohmann::ordered_json
  • nlohmann::ordered_json_document
  • nlohmann::ordered_json_view
  • nlohmann::ordered_map
  • nlohmann::to_string
  • nlohmann::literals::json_literals::operator""_json
  • nlohmann::literals::json_literals::operator""_json_pointer

The module always exports the two user-defined string literals, even if JSON_NO_AUTOMATIC_UDLS is defined when building it.

Additionally, the following nlohmann::detail symbols are exported, solely to work around an MSVC compilation issue (#3970). They are implementation details, not part of the public API, and should not be used directly:

  • nlohmann::detail::json_sax_dom_callback_parser
  • nlohmann::detail::unknown_size

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
C++20 modules support is exercised in CI against current GCC and Clang on Ubuntu, and the default MSVC toolset on Windows Server 2022 — there is no documented minimum compiler version, unlike feature-test-macro-gated features such as JSON_HAS_RANGES.

Known compiler issues

  • GCC may emit "redefinition" errors when #include <nlohmann/json.hpp> appears in a module preamble together with other imports. This is an upstream GCC bug, not yet resolved as of GCC 16. Workarounds: include nlohmann/json.hpp before other #includes, use import nlohmann.json; instead, or upgrade GCC. (issue #5103)
  • MSVC could fail with C2039: 'json_sax_dom_callback_parser' is not a member of ... detail; fixed by exporting the required internal symbols from json.cppm (see Exported symbols above). (issue #3970)

If you hit a different module-related build failure, search existing issues before filing a new one.

docs.title: See also

docs.title: nlohmann Namespace
docs.text: The 3.11.0 release introduced an inline namespace to allow different parts of a codebase to safely use different versions of the JSON library as long as they never exchange instances of library types.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The complete default namespace name is derived as follows:

  • The root namespace is always nlohmann.
  • The inline namespace starts with json_abi and is followed by several optional ABI tags according to the value of these ABI-affecting macros, in order:
    • JSON_DIAGNOSTICS defined non-zero appends _diag.
    • JSON_USE_LEGACY_DISCARDED_VALUE_COMPARISON defined non-zero appends _ldvcmp.
    • JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS defined non-zero appends _dp.
    • JSON_BRACE_INIT_COPY_SEMANTICS defined non-zero appends _bics.
    • JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION defined non-zero appends _psp.
    • JSON_STRICT_NUL_HANDLING defined non-zero appends _snul.
    • JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8 defined non-zero appends _sbu8.
    • JSON_USE_OBJECTS_FOR_ENUM_KEYED_MAPS defined non-zero appends _ekmo.
    • JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN defined non-zero appends _dsbs.
    • JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO defined non-zero appends _dufio.
    • JSON_NO_SIMD defined appends _ns.
  • The inline namespace ends with the suffix _v followed by the 3 components of the version number separated by underscores. To omit the version component, see Disabling the version component below.

For example, the namespace name for version 3.11.2 with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS defined to 1 is:

nlohmann::json_abi_diag_v3_11_2

The name is assembled from these segments; pick a version and macros to see the resulting name:

nlohmannroot namespace :: json_abialways _diagJSON_DIAGNOSTICS=1 _v3_11_2version 3.11.2 Version 3.11.2 with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS defined to 1. ABI tags are appended in the order of the list above, the version suffix comes last.

The name of the inline namespace, assembled from its segments. Select a version and macros to see which ABI tags appear; a tag the chosen version does not have is disabled.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Several incompatibilities have been observed. Amongst the most common ones is linking code compiled with different definitions of JSON_DIAGNOSTICS. This is illustrated in the diagram below.

graph
    json["<strong>nlohmann_json (v3.10.5)</strong><br>JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=0"]
    json_diag["<strong>nlohmann_json (v3.10.5)</strong><br>JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=1"]
    library["<strong>some library</strong>"]
    app["<strong>application</strong>"]

    library --> json
    app --> json_diag
    app --> library

The application uses the library with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=1 and links some library, which uses the same library version with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=0. Arrows point from a component to what it uses.

In releases prior to 3.11.0, mixing any version of the JSON library with different JSON_DIAGNOSTICS settings would result in a crashing application. If some_library never passes instances of JSON library types to the application, this scenario became safe in version 3.11.0 and above due to the inline namespace yielding distinct symbol names.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Neither the compiler nor the linker will issue as much as a warning when translation units – intended to be linked together and that include different versions and/or configurations of the JSON library – exchange and use library types.

There is an exception when forward declarations are used (i.e., when including json_fwd.hpp) in which case the linker may complain about undefined references.

docs.title: Disabling the version component
docs.text:
Different versions are not necessarily ABI-incompatible, but the project does not actively track changes in the ABI and recommends that all parts of a codebase exchanging library types be built with the same version. Users can, at their own risk, disable the version component of the inline namespace, allowing different versions – but not configurations – to be used in cases where the linker would otherwise output undefined reference errors.

To do so, define NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_NO_VERSION to 1.

This applies to version 3.11.2 and above only; versions 3.11.0 and 3.11.1 can apply the technique described in the next section to emulate the effect of the NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_NO_VERSION macro.

Use at your own risk

Disabling the namespace version component and mixing ABI-incompatible versions will result in crashes or incorrect behavior. You have been warned!

docs.title: Disabling the inline namespace completely
docs.text:
When interoperability with code using a pre-3.11.0 version of the library is required, users can, at their own risk restore the old namespace layout by redefining NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_BEGIN, NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_END as follows:

#define NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_BEGIN  namespace nlohmann {
#define NLOHMANN_JSON_NAMESPACE_END    }

Use at your own risk

Overriding the namespace and mixing ABI-incompatible versions will result in crashes or incorrect behavior. You have been warned!

docs.title: Working Without Exceptions
docs.text: By default, the library reports errors by throwing exceptions (see Exceptions). This page collects what to use when exceptions are unwanted or unavailable, for example in embedded systems, game engines, or code compiled with -fno-exceptions.

docs.title: Two different questions
docs.text:
1. Can my code avoid catching exceptions? Yes. For parsing and for accessing values there are functions that report failure through a return value. They work in a normal build and need no try/catch.
  2. Can the library be compiled without exceptions? Yes, with -fno-exceptions or by defining JSON_NOEXCEPTION. Both have the same effect: every throw in the library becomes a call to std::abort(). The functions listed below never reach a throw for the failures they report, so they keep working in this configuration. Anything else that fails aborts the program.

docs.title: Parsing
Accessing values
docs.text:
The access functions are not equally safe. Only some of them never throw:

expression if the key is missing or the type is wrong j.contains("k") returns false for a missing key; never throws j.find("k") returns end() for a missing key; never throws j.is_string(), ... the is_* functions test the type; never throw j.get_ptr<const std::string*>() returns nullptr for a different type; never throws j.at("k") throws out_of_range.403 for a missing key j.get<int>() throws type_error.302 for a value that is not a number j.value("k", 0) returns the default for a missing key, but throws type_error.302 if k exists with another type j["k"] (non-const) inserts null for a missing key j["k"] (const) undefined behavior for a missing key

So reading a value that may be absent or of the wrong type without exceptions takes two steps: look up, then test the type.

Example: look up a key and test its type 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    json j = json::parse(R"({"name": "Mary", "age": 42})");

    // look up the key, then test the type: neither step throws
    const auto keys = {"name", "age", "city"};
    for (const char* key : keys)
    {
        const auto it = j.find(key);
        if (it == j.end())
        {
            std::cout << key << ": missing\n";
        }
        else if (it->is_string())
        {
            std::cout << key << ": string \"" << it->get_ref<const std::string&>() << "\"\n";
        }
        else
        {
            std::cout << key << ": not a string, but " << it->type_name() << '\n';
        }
    }

    // get_ptr returns a null pointer if the value has another type
    const std::string* name = j["name"].get_ptr<const std::string*>();
    const std::string* age = j["age"].get_ptr<const std::string*>();
    std::cout << "get_ptr<string*>: name = " << (name != nullptr) << ", age = " << (age != nullptr) << '\n';

    // value() is NOT exception-free: it throws if the key exists with a different type
    try
    {
        std::cout << j.value("name", 0) << '\n';
    }
    catch (const json::type_error& e)
    {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

name: string "Mary"
age: not a string, but number
city: missing
get_ptr<string*>: name = 1, age = 0
[json.exception.type_error.302] type must be number, but is string

The last lines of the example show why value is not on the safe list: it returns the default only for a missing key.

For numbers, test with is_number() (or is_number_integer(), is_number_unsigned(), is_number_float()) before calling get<int>(), and see number handling for range and precision. Whether a value fits into the target type is not checked by get.

docs.title: Converting to your own types
docs.text:
from_json functions (including the ones generated by the NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_* macros) report problems by throwing. There is no variant that returns an error code. Without exceptions you have two options:

  • Validate the JSON value yourself, as shown above, and fill your struct field by field.
  • Convert in a function that is compiled with exceptions enabled and catches them at the boundary, returning std::optional or an error code to the rest of your code:
Example: convert to a struct and report failure as std::optional 
#include <iostream>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

struct person
{
    std::string name;
    int age;
};

NLOHMANN_DEFINE_TYPE_NON_INTRUSIVE(person, name, age)

// Compile this function with exceptions enabled and call it from code that does not use them.
std::optional<person> to_person(const json& j)
{
    try
    {
        return j.get<person>();
    }
    catch (const json::exception&)
    {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
}

int main()
{
    const json good = {{"name", "Mary"}, {"age", 42}};
    const json bad = {{"name", "Mary"}, {"age", "forty-two"}};
    const json incomplete = {{"name", "Mary"}};

    const auto inputs = {good, bad, incomplete};

    for (const json& j : inputs)
    {
        if (const auto p = to_person(j))
        {
            std::cout << "person: " << p->name << ", " << p->age << '\n';
        }
        else
        {
            std::cout << "not a person: " << j << '\n';
        }
    }
}

Output:

person: Mary, 42
not a person: {"age":"forty-two","name":"Mary"}
not a person: {"name":"Mary"}

docs.title: Overriding what happens instead of an exception
docs.text: With exceptions off, you can replace the abort() by your own code, for example to log the message first. See Switch off exceptions and JSON_THROW_USER. The handler must not return normally.

docs.title: Object Order
docs.text: The JSON standard defines objects as "an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs". As such, an implementation does not need to preserve any specific order of object keys.

docs.title: Default behavior: sort keys
docs.text:
The default type nlohmann::json uses a std::map to store JSON objects, and thus stores object keys sorted alphabetically.

Example: json sorts object keys 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    json j;
    j["one"] = 1;
    j["two"] = 2;
    j["three"] = 3;

    std::cout << j.dump(2) << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "one": 1,
  "three": 3,
  "two": 2
}

docs.title: Alternative behavior: preserve insertion order
docs.text:
If you do want to preserve the insertion order, you can use the type nlohmann::ordered_json.

Example: ordered_json preserves insertion order 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::ordered_json;

int main()
{
    ordered_json j;
    j["one"] = 1;
    j["two"] = 2;
    j["three"] = 3;

    std::cout << j.dump(2) << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "one": 1,
  "two": 2,
  "three": 3
}

Alternatively, nlohmann::fifo_map also preserves the insertion order and, unlike ordered_map, keeps a lookup index, so it does not have the quadratic cost described below. It is used through a small adapter (integration).

If the order does not matter and you only want faster lookup, boost::unordered_flat_map, absl::flat_hash_map, absl::node_hash_map, and several other hash maps work through an adapter that restores the template argument order basic_json expects; see Template Parameter Requirements. Note these are unordered, not insertion-ordered.

tsl::ordered_map cannot be used: its iterators expose the mapped value as const, while basic_json needs to modify it in place.

The ordered_map behind nlohmann::ordered_json is deliberately minimal and has no lookup index, so every key access is a linear scan and building an object of n keys costs O(n²). This is unnoticeable at typical object sizes but becomes significant for objects with many thousands of keys; see ordered_map complexity. The alternatives above keep a lookup index and do not have this cost.

docs.title: Notes on parsing
docs.text:
Note that you also need to call the right parse function when reading from a file. Assume file input.json contains the JSON object above:

{
  "one": 1,
  "two": 2,
  "three": 3
}

Right way

The following code correctly calls the parse function from nlohmann::ordered_json:

std::ifstream i("input.json");
auto j = nlohmann::ordered_json::parse(i);
std::cout << j.dump(2) << std::endl;

The output will be:

{
  "one": 1,
  "two": 2,
  "three": 3
}
Wrong way

The following code incorrectly calls the parse function from nlohmann::json which does not preserve the insertion order, but sorts object keys. Assigning the result to nlohmann::ordered_json compiles, but does not restore the order from the input file.

std::ifstream i("input.json");
nlohmann::ordered_json j = nlohmann::json::parse(i);
std::cout << j.dump(2) << std::endl;

The output will be:

{
  "one": 1,
  "three": 3,
  "two": 2
}
