bytes follow) 0x9A array size: 4294967296..18446744073709551615 array (8 bytes follow) 0x9B object size: 0..23 map 0xA0..0xB7 object size: 24..255 map (1 byte follow) 0xB8 object size: 256..65535 map (2 bytes follow) 0xB9 object size: 65536..4294967295 map (4 bytes follow) 0xBA object size: 4294967296..18446744073709551615 map (8 bytes follow) 0xBB binary size: 0..23 byte string 0x40..0x57 binary size: 24..255 byte string (1 byte follow) 0x58 binary size: 256..65535 byte string (2 bytes follow) 0x59 binary size: 65536..4294967295 byte string (4 bytes follow) 0x5A binary size: 4294967296..18446744073709551615 byte string (8 bytes follow) 0x5B

Binary values with subtype are mapped to tagged values (0xD8..0xDB) depending on the subtype, followed by a byte string, see "binary" cells in the table above.

Complete mapping

The mapping is complete in the sense that any JSON value type can be converted to a CBOR value, with one exception: an integer outside the range of CBOR integers (only possible with a number type wider than 64 bits) throws out_of_range.407.

Not a deterministic encoding

to_cbor does not produce the deterministic encoding of RFC 8949, Section 4.2.1, and not always the preferred serialization of Section 4.1:

  • floating-point numbers are written as single precision (0xFA) when that is exact and as double precision (0xFB) otherwise; half precision (0xF9) is used only for NaN and Infinity/-Infinity (1.0 is fa 3f 80 00 00);
  • a binary subtype 0..23 is written as d8 xx instead of the one-byte tag 0xC0..0xD7 (d8 01 41 01);
  • object members are written in the order of object_t (for the default std::map: sorted by the key string, not by the encoded key bytes).

Integers and lengths use the shortest form, and indefinite-length items are never written. Decoders must accept all of this; the RFC does not require the preferred serialization.

NaN/infinity handling

NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity are serialized as a CBOR half-precision float (type 0xF9, 3 bytes total): NaN as 0xF9 0x7E 0x00, Infinity as 0xF9 0x7C 0x00, and -Infinity as 0xF9 0xFC 0x00. This behavior differs from the normal JSON serialization which serializes NaN or Infinity to null.

Note

Prior to version 3.8.0, NaN and Infinity were instead serialized as a CBOR double-precision float (type 0xFB, 9 bytes total).

Unused CBOR types

The following CBOR types are not used in the conversion:

  • UTF-8 strings terminated by "break" (0x7F)
  • arrays terminated by "break" (0x9F)
  • maps terminated by "break" (0xBF)
  • byte strings terminated by "break" (0x5F)
  • date/time (0xC0..0xC1)
  • bignum (0xC2..0xC3)
  • decimal fraction (0xC4)
  • bigfloat (0xC5)
  • expected conversions (0xD5..0xD7)
  • simple values (0xE0..0xF3, 0xF8)
  • undefined (0xF7)
  • break (0xFF)

Tagged items

Binary subtypes will be serialized as tagged items. See binary values for an example.

Example: serialize a JSON value to CBOR 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;
using namespace nlohmann::literals;

int main()
{
    // create a JSON value
    json j = R"({"compact": true, "schema": 0})"_json;

    // serialize it to CBOR
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = json::to_cbor(j);

    // print the vector content
    for (auto& byte : v)
    {
        std::cout << "0x" << std::hex << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << static_cast<int>(byte) << " ";
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

0xa2 0x67 0x63 0x6f 0x6d 0x70 0x61 0x63 0x74 0xf5 0x66 0x73 0x63 0x68 0x65 0x6d 0x61 0x00

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
The library maps CBOR types to JSON value types as follows:

CBOR type JSON value type first byte Integer number_unsigned 0x00..0x17 Unsigned integer number_unsigned 0x18 Unsigned integer number_unsigned 0x19 Unsigned integer number_unsigned 0x1A Unsigned integer number_unsigned 0x1B Negative integer number_integer 0x20..0x37 Negative integer number_integer 0x38 Negative integer number_integer 0x39 Negative integer number_integer 0x3A Negative integer number_integer 0x3B Byte string binary 0x40..0x57 Byte string binary 0x58 Byte string binary 0x59 Byte string binary 0x5A Byte string binary 0x5B Byte string binary 0x5F UTF-8 string string 0x60..0x77 UTF-8 string string 0x78 UTF-8 string string 0x79 UTF-8 string string 0x7A UTF-8 string string 0x7B UTF-8 string string 0x7F array array 0x80..0x97 array array 0x98 array array 0x99 array array 0x9A array array 0x9B array array 0x9F map object 0xA0..0xB7 map object 0xB8 map object 0xB9 map object 0xBA map object 0xBB map object 0xBF False false 0xF4 True true 0xF5 Null null 0xF6 Half-Precision Float number_float 0xF9 Single-Precision Float number_float 0xFA Double-Precision Float number_float 0xFB

Indefinite-length UTF-8 strings (0x7F) and byte strings (0x5F) are supported. Each chunk must be a definite-length string of the same major type, as required by RFC 8949, Section 3.2.3.

Incomplete mapping

The mapping is incomplete in the sense that not all CBOR types can be converted to a JSON value. The following CBOR types are not supported and will yield parse errors:

  • simple values (0xE0..0xF3, 0xF8)
  • undefined (0xF7)

Tagged items (0xC0..0xDB) are not interpreted either; see the note on tagged items below.

Negative integer overflow

CBOR negative integers (major type 1) are decoded as -1 - n. If the encoded magnitude n is too large for the result to fit into number_integer_t (std::int64_t by default), the result is stored as number_float_t, like a too small integer in JSON text. For example, -18446744073709551616 (0x3B followed by eight 0xFF bytes) is stored as -1.8446744073709552e+19.

Object keys

CBOR allows map keys of any type, whereas JSON only allows strings as keys in object values. Therefore, CBOR maps with keys other than text strings (major type 3) are rejected with a parse_error.113 exception (or, with allow_exceptions set to false, a discarded value) naming the type of the key that was found, for instance:

[json.exception.parse_error.113] parse error at byte 2: syntax error while parsing CBOR object key: only string keys are supported, but found an unsigned integer; last byte: 0x01

This applies to the SAX interface as well, as the key is read before it is passed on. This is a deliberate restriction of the library's JSON value model, not an oversight: formats built on CBOR maps with integer keys, such as COSE (RFC 9052) or CWT (RFC 8392), cannot be read with this library and need a general-purpose CBOR library instead.

A tag in front of a text string key is handled like a tag in front of a value: it is skipped with cbor_tag_handler_t::ignore or cbor_tag_handler_t::store and rejected with the default error. A tag does not turn a key of another type into a text string.

A map with duplicate keys is well-formed, but invalid under RFC 8949, Section 5.3.1. from_cbor accepts it and the last value wins; the SAX interface reports every occurrence.

Ill-formed UTF-8 in text strings

RFC 8949, Section 3.1 requires CBOR text strings (major type 3) to be valid UTF-8 (a string with ill-formed UTF-8 is "well-formed but invalid"), and Section 5.3.1 leaves it up to the decoder whether to verify this, so checking is opt-in: with the error_handler parameter left at keep (the default), from_cbor() accepts a text string (object keys included) whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 and hands them back unchanged. Passing error_handler_t::strict makes from_cbor() check and throw parse_error.113 for ill-formed UTF-8, and replace/ignore sanitize the string instead of keeping it. However, dump() still requires valid UTF-8 and throws type_error.316 for a value read with the default keep handler, unless an error handler is passed that replaces or ignores the ill-formed bytes. to_cbor()'s own error_handler parameter defaults to keep, so such a value is written back unchanged; with strict (the default if JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8 is enabled), it throws the same exception instead. Byte strings (major type 2) are unaffected, since they are not required to hold text.

The chunks of an indefinite-length text string are checked one by one, as required by RFC 8949, Section 3.2.3: a code point cannot be spread over two chunks. With error_handler_t::strict such a string throws parse_error.113; replace and ignore sanitize each chunk on its own.

Tagged items

Tagged items (0xC0..0xDB) will throw a parse error by default. They can be ignored by passing cbor_tag_handler_t::ignore to function from_cbor, in which case the tag is skipped and the enclosed data item is parsed on its own. Passing cbor_tag_handler_t::store to function from_cbor stores tagged byte strings (for bytes 0xd8..0xdb) as binary values with the tag as subtype; other tagged values are read as if the tag were ignored. If several tags precede a byte string, only the tag directly in front of it is stored, and only when it has the form 0xD8..0xDB (a tag 0..23 written as 0xC0..0xD7 is skipped); for example, D8 05 C1 41 AA yields subtype null, whereas C1 D8 05 41 AA yields 5. Tags in front of a text string map key are skipped as well. Note that no tag is ever interpreted: for instance, a text string tagged with tag 0 (date/time) stays a string.

Example: deserialize a JSON value from CBOR 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    // create byte vector
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = {0xa2, 0x67, 0x63, 0x6f, 0x6d, 0x70, 0x61, 0x63,
                                   0x74, 0xf5, 0x66, 0x73, 0x63, 0x68, 0x65, 0x6d,
                                   0x61, 0x00
                                  };

    // deserialize it with CBOR
    json j = json::from_cbor(v);

    // print the deserialized JSON value
    std::cout << std::setw(2) << j << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "compact": true,
  "schema": 0
}

docs.title: MessagePack
docs.text:
MessagePack is an efficient binary serialization format. It lets you exchange data among multiple languages like JSON. But it's faster and smaller. Small integers are encoded into a single byte, and typical short strings require only one extra byte in addition to the strings themselves.

References

  • MessagePack website
  • MessagePack specification

docs.title: Byte layout
docs.text:
MessagePack encodes each value as a one-byte format marker, optionally followed by a length or the payload. The marker range is partitioned to keep common values small: small non-negative integers (0 to 127) and small negative integers (-32 to -1) are the marker byte itself; short strings, arrays, and maps (up to 31 bytes for strings and up to 15 elements for arrays and maps) hide their length in the marker's lower bits. Larger values use dedicated markers that announce the width (8, 16, 32, or 64 bits) of the length or number that follows, in big-endian byte order. Like CBOR, containers are length-prefixed, so no terminator is needed.

Consider the following JSON value (shown formatted for readability):

{
  "id": 300,
  "name": "json",
  "pi": 3.14,
  "tags": [
    "a",
    "b"
  ]
}

to_msgpack encodes it to 39 bytes (shown in hexadecimal; the encoding contains no whitespace). The colors mark the role of each byte: type/marker data.

JSONBytesMeaning {84map with 4 key/value pairs "id": 300,A2 69 64 CD 01 2Ckey: fixstr of length 2, then its UTF-8 bytes; value: uint 16 (big-endian) "name": "json",A4 6E 61 6D 65 A4 6A 73 6F 6Ekey: fixstr of length 4; value: fixstr of length 4 "pi": 3.14,A2 70 69 CB 40 09 1E B8 51 EB 85 1Fkey: fixstr of length 2; value: float 64 (IEEE 754, big-endian) "tags": [A4 74 61 67 73 92key: fixstr of length 4; value: fixarray with 2 elements "a",A1 61fixstr of length 1 "b"A1 62fixstr of length 1 ]no end marker: the element count was given up front }no end marker: the member count was given up front

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
The library uses the following mapping from JSON values types to MessagePack types according to the MessagePack specification:

JSON value type value/range MessagePack type first byte null null nil 0xC0 boolean true true 0xC3 boolean false false 0xC2 number_integer -9223372036854775808..-2147483649 int64 0xD3 number_integer -2147483648..-32769 int32 0xD2 number_integer -32768..-129 int16 0xD1 number_integer -128..-33 int8 0xD0 number_integer -32..-1 negative fixint 0xE0..0xFF number_integer 0..127 positive fixint 0x00..0x7F number_integer 128..255 uint 8 0xCC number_integer 256..65535 uint 16 0xCD number_integer 65536..4294967295 uint 32 0xCE number_integer 4294967296..18446744073709551615 uint 64 0xCF number_unsigned 0..127 positive fixint 0x00..0x7F number_unsigned 128..255 uint 8 0xCC number_unsigned 256..65535 uint 16 0xCD number_unsigned 65536..4294967295 uint 32 0xCE number_unsigned 4294967296..18446744073709551615 uint 64 0xCF number_float any value representable by a float float 32 0xCA number_float any value NOT representable by a float float 64 0xCB string length: 0..31 fixstr 0xA0..0xBF string length: 32..255 str 8 0xD9 string length: 256..65535 str 16 0xDA string length: 65536..4294967295 str 32 0xDB array size: 0..15 fixarray 0x90..0x9F array size: 16..65535 array 16 0xDC array size: 65536..4294967295 array 32 0xDD object size: 0..15 fix map 0x80..0x8F object size: 16..65535 map 16 0xDE object size: 65536..4294967295 map 32 0xDF binary size: 0..255 bin 8 0xC4 binary size: 256..65535 bin 16 0xC5 binary size: 65536..4294967295 bin 32 0xC6

Complete mapping

The mapping is complete in the sense that any JSON value type can be converted to a MessagePack value.

Any MessagePack output created by to_msgpack can be successfully parsed by from_msgpack.

Size constraints

The following values can not be converted to a MessagePack value:

  • strings with more than 4294967295 bytes
  • byte strings with more than 4294967295 bytes
  • arrays with more than 4294967295 elements
  • objects with more than 4294967295 elements

Serializing such a value throws out_of_range.412.

NaN/infinity handling

NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity are serialized as a MessagePack float 32 (type 0xCA, 5 bytes total), regardless of magnitude, in contrast to the dump function which serializes NaN or Infinity to null.

Note

Prior to version 3.13.0 unreleased, NaN and Infinity were instead serialized as a MessagePack float 64 (type 0xCB, 9 bytes total), because the check used to select the smaller float 32 encoding failed for NaN (all comparisons are false) and for Infinity and -Infinity (outside the float range checked against std::numeric_limits<float>::lowest() and max()), so the float 32 path was skipped.

Example: serialize a JSON value to MessagePack 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;
using namespace nlohmann::literals;

int main()
{
    // create a JSON value
    json j = R"({"compact": true, "schema": 0})"_json;

    // serialize it to MessagePack
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = json::to_msgpack(j);

    // print the vector content
    for (auto& byte : v)
    {
        std::cout << "0x" << std::hex << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << static_cast<int>(byte) << " ";
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

0x82 0xa7 0x63 0x6f 0x6d 0x70 0x61 0x63 0x74 0xc3 0xa6 0x73 0x63 0x68 0x65 0x6d 0x61 0x00

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
The library maps MessagePack types to JSON value types as follows:

MessagePack type JSON value type first byte positive fixint number_unsigned 0x00..0x7F fixmap object 0x80..0x8F fixarray array 0x90..0x9F fixstr string 0xA0..0xBF nil null 0xC0 (never used) – 0xC1 false false 0xC2 true true 0xC3 float 32 number_float 0xCA float 64 number_float 0xCB uint 8 number_unsigned 0xCC uint 16 number_unsigned 0xCD uint 32 number_unsigned 0xCE uint 64 number_unsigned 0xCF int 8 number_integer 0xD0 int 16 number_integer 0xD1 int 32 number_integer 0xD2 int 64 number_integer 0xD3 str 8 string 0xD9 str 16 string 0xDA str 32 string 0xDB array 16 array 0xDC array 32 array 0xDD map 16 object 0xDE map 32 object 0xDF bin 8 binary 0xC4 bin 16 binary 0xC5 bin 32 binary 0xC6 ext 8 binary 0xC7 ext 16 binary 0xC8 ext 32 binary 0xC9 fixext 1 binary 0xD4 fixext 2 binary 0xD5 fixext 4 binary 0xD6 fixext 8 binary 0xD7 fixext 16 binary 0xD8 negative fixint number_integer 0xE0-0xFF

The byte 0xC1 is reserved as "never used" by the specification. As a value it is rejected with parse_error.112 (invalid byte: 0xC1); as a map key it is rejected with parse_error.113 and the generic "expected length specification" message, because the key is read as a string.

Duplicate keys in a map are accepted; the last value wins.

docs.title: Extension types (ext, fixext)
docs.text:
MessagePack ext and fixext values are read as binary values, and the ext type byte is stored as the binary subtype. Although the specification defines the type as a signed 8-bit integer (0 to 127 for applications, -128 to -1 reserved, with -1 being the Timestamp extension), the library reads it as an unsigned byte: a negative ext type n becomes subtype 256+n, so ext type -1 is read as subtype 255 and -128 as subtype 128. The Timestamp extension is not interpreted; it is returned as binary with subtype 255. Use has_subtype() to tell a bin value (no subtype) from an ext value (subtype, even if it is 0).

When serializing, a binary value with a subtype is always written as fixext (1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 bytes) or ext, even for subtype 0 (d6 00 01 02 03 04); a binary value without a subtype is written as bin. Subtypes 128 to 255 are written as the reserved negative ext types (255 as -1), so json::binary({1,2,3,4}, 255) becomes d6 ff 01 02 03 04, which other MessagePack libraries decode as a 32-bit timestamp. A subtype above 255 throws out_of_range.415. The payload length is limited to 4294967295 bytes like all other lengths.

Info

Any MessagePack output created by to_msgpack can be successfully parsed by from_msgpack.

Object keys

MessagePack allows map keys of any type, whereas JSON only allows strings as keys in object values. Like the JSON-compatible profile sketched in the MessagePack specification, this library restricts map keys to str values. Maps with keys of any other type are rejected with a parse_error.113 exception (or, with allow_exceptions set to false, a discarded value). For most key types the message names the type that was found, for instance:

[json.exception.parse_error.113] parse error at byte 2: syntax error while parsing MessagePack object key: only string keys are supported, but found nil; last byte: 0xC0

This applies to the SAX interface as well, as the key is read before it is passed on. Such input needs a general-purpose MessagePack library instead.

Ill-formed UTF-8 in string values

The MessagePack specification explicitly allows a str value (fixstr, str 8, str 16, str 32) to contain a byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8, and recommends that a deserializer provide a way to obtain the original bytes. This library follows that by default: with its error_handler parameter left at keep (the default), from_msgpack() reads str bytes (object keys included) as-is, without validating them, so such a value round-trips through from_msgpack(to_msgpack(j)) byte for byte. Passing error_handler_t::strict makes from_msgpack() check anyway and throw parse_error.113 for ill-formed UTF-8, and replace/ignore sanitize the string instead of keeping it. to_msgpack() also writes str bytes as-is by default, since the specification permits it; its error_handler parameter can be set to strict to throw type_error.316 instead, or to replace/ignore to sanitize the string, for instance for a decoder that rejects ill-formed UTF-8. However, dump() still requires valid UTF-8 and throws type_error.316 for a value read this way with the default keep handler, unless an error handler is passed that replaces or ignores the ill-formed bytes.

Example: deserialize a JSON value from MessagePack 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    // create byte vector
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = {0x82, 0xa7, 0x63, 0x6f, 0x6d, 0x70, 0x61, 0x63,
                                   0x74, 0xc3, 0xa6, 0x73, 0x63, 0x68, 0x65, 0x6d,
                                   0x61, 0x00
                                  };

    // deserialize it with MessagePack
    json j = json::from_msgpack(v);

    // print the deserialized JSON value
    std::cout << std::setw(2) << j << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "compact": true,
  "schema": 0
}

docs.title: UBJSON
docs.text:
Universal Binary JSON (UBJSON) is a binary form directly imitating JSON, but requiring fewer bytes of data. It aims to achieve the generality of JSON, combined with being much easier to process than JSON.

References

  • UBJSON Website

docs.title: Byte layout
docs.text:
UBJSON is built from just a one-byte, human-readable ASCII type marker (for example, i for int8, S for string, [ for array) followed by the payload of that type. Strings and the like are prefixed with their length, which is itself a UBJSON integer value including its marker. Numbers are stored in big-endian byte order. Containers can be written in two ways: as an unoptimized container that is opened with [ or { and closed with ] or }, or as an optimized container that declares a count (#) after the opening marker, optionally preceded by an element type ($); an element type is only allowed together with a count. An optimized container saves the closing marker and, with a type, the per-element markers.

Consider the following JSON value (shown formatted for readability):

{
  "id": 300,
  "name": "json",
  "pi": 3.14,
  "tags": [
    "a",
    "b"
  ]
}

to_ubjson encodes it to 51 bytes (shown in hexadecimal; the encoding contains no whitespace). The colors mark the role of each byte: type/marker length/count/size data.

JSONBytesMeaning {7Bobject start ({) "id": 300,69 02 69 64 49 01 2Ckey: length 2 as int8 (i), then UTF-8 bytes; value: int16 (I), big-endian "name": "json",69 04 6E 61 6D 65 53 69 04 6A 73 6F 6Ekey: length 4; value: string (S), length 4 as int8, UTF-8 bytes "pi": 3.14,69 02 70 69 44 40 09 1E B8 51 EB 85 1Fkey: length 2; value: float64 (D), big-endian "tags": [69 04 74 61 67 73 5Bkey: length 4; value: array start ([) "a",53 69 01 61string, length 1 "b"53 69 01 62string, length 1 ]5Darray end (]) }7Dobject end (})

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
The library uses the following mapping from JSON values types to UBJSON types according to the UBJSON specification:

JSON value type value/range UBJSON type marker null null null Z boolean true true T boolean false false F number_integer -9223372036854775808..-2147483649 int64 L number_integer -2147483648..-32769 int32 l number_integer -32768..-129 int16 I number_integer -128..127 int8 i number_integer 128..255 uint8 U number_integer 256..32767 int16 I number_integer 32768..2147483647 int32 l number_integer 2147483648..9223372036854775807 int64 L number_unsigned 0..127 int8 i number_unsigned 128..255 uint8 U number_unsigned 256..32767 int16 I number_unsigned 32768..2147483647 int32 l number_unsigned 2147483648..9223372036854775807 int64 L number_unsigned 9223372036854775808..18446744073709551615 high-precision H number_float any value float64 (float32 if number_float_t is float) D (d) string with shortest length indicator string S array see notes on optimized format array [ object see notes on optimized format object {

Complete mapping

The mapping is complete in the sense that any JSON value type can be converted to a UBJSON value.

Any UBJSON output created by to_ubjson can be successfully parsed by from_ubjson.

Size constraints

The following values can not be converted to a UBJSON value:

  • strings with more than 9223372036854775807 bytes (theoretical)

UTF-8 validation of string values and object keys

UBJSON's required string encoding is UTF-8. By default (the error_handler parameter left at keep), to_ubjson() writes the bytes of string values and object keys unchanged, even if they are not valid UTF-8. With error_handler_t::strict, it throws type_error.316 for ill-formed UTF-8 instead; replace/ignore sanitize the string. JSON_STRICT_BINARY_UTF8 makes strict the default.

Unused UBJSON markers

The following markers are not used in the conversion:

  • N: no-op values are never written (they are skipped when reading).
  • C: single-byte strings are serialized with S markers.

NaN/infinity handling

NaN and infinity are written as IEEE 754 float64 values (D) and read back unchanged. This differs from dump(), which serializes them to null, and from the UBJSON specification, which encodes infinity as null (it does not mention NaN); other UBJSON readers may therefore not accept these values.

Optimized formats

The optimized formats for containers are supported: Parameter use_size adds size information to the beginning of a container and removes the closing marker. Parameter use_type further checks whether all elements of a container have the same type and adds the type marker to the beginning of the container. The use_type parameter must only be used together with use_size = true: combining use_type with use_size = false throws other_error.502 if the value contains a non-empty array, object, or binary value.

Two elements have the same type if they are written with the same type marker. For example, [1, 2] is written with the type i, but [1, 200] (i, U), [true, false] (T, F), and [1, 2.5] (i, D) are not; an empty container is never given a $ annotation of its own (an array of empty arrays is still typed [).

Note that use_size = true alone may result in larger representations - the benefit of this parameter is that the receiving side is immediately informed on the number of elements of the container.

An array whose type marker is Z (null), T (true) or F (false) stores no payload at all, because the marker already is the value. Its declared count is therefore the only thing that decides how much memory the receiving side allocates, and a handful of bytes can describe billions of elements. from_ubjson rejects such an array with out_of_range.408 when the count exceeds 1,048,576 (1 << 20), and to_ubjson writes longer arrays of these types in the counted but untyped form: the $ type marker is dropped, the # count is kept, and every element is written with its own marker ([#l 1048577 Z Z ...), so any value it produces can be read back. Objects and untyped counted arrays are not subject to this limit.

Binary values

If the JSON data contains the binary type, the value stored is a list of integers, as suggested by the UBJSON documentation. In particular, this means that serialization and the deserialization of a JSON containing binary values into UBJSON and back will result in a different JSON object.

Example: serialize JSON values to UBJSON, with and without size/type optimization 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;
using namespace nlohmann::literals;

// function to print UBJSON's diagnostic format
void print_byte(uint8_t byte)
{
    if (32 < byte and byte < 128)
    {
        std::cout << static_cast<char>(byte);
    }
    else
    {
        std::cout << static_cast<int>(byte);
    }
}

int main()
{
    // create a JSON value
    json j = R"({"compact": true, "schema": false})"_json;

    // serialize it to UBJSON
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = json::to_ubjson(j);

    // print the vector content
    for (auto& byte : v)
    {
        print_byte(byte);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';

    // create an array of numbers
    json array = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8};

    // serialize it to UBJSON using default representation
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v_array = json::to_ubjson(array);
    // serialize it to UBJSON using size optimization
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v_array_size = json::to_ubjson(array, true);
    // serialize it to UBJSON using type optimization
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v_array_size_and_type = json::to_ubjson(array, true, true);

    // print the vector contents
    for (auto& byte : v_array)
    {
        print_byte(byte);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';

    for (auto& byte : v_array_size)
    {
        print_byte(byte);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';

    for (auto& byte : v_array_size_and_type)
    {
        print_byte(byte);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
}

Output:

{i7compactTi6schemaF}
[i1i2i3i4i5i6i7i8]
[#i8i1i2i3i4i5i6i7i8
[$i#i812345678

docs.title: Deserialization
docs.text:
The library maps UBJSON types to JSON value types as follows:

UBJSON type JSON value type marker no-op no value, next value is read N null null Z false false F true true T float32 number_float d float64 number_float D uint8 number_unsigned U int8 number_integer i int16 number_integer I int32 number_integer l int64 number_integer L string string S char string C high-precision number_unsigned, number_integer, or number_float H array array (optimized values are supported) [ object object (optimized values are supported) {

High-precision numbers

The payload of H is a length-prefixed string that is parsed as a JSON number (surrounding whitespace is ignored). Integer text in the range of number_unsigned_t (non-negative) or number_integer_t (negative) is stored as such; any other valid number text (larger or smaller integers, fractions, and exponents such as 1e2) is stored as number_float, so precision may be lost. Text that is not a valid JSON number raises parse_error.115, a number outside the range of number_float_t (1e999) raises out_of_range.406.

Complete mapping

Every well-formed UBJSON value can be converted to a JSON value, with these exceptions: a high-precision number outside the range of number_float_t (out_of_range.406), an optimized array of Z, T, or F with more than 1,048,576 elements, and a count that exceeds the capacity of the container (out_of_range.408). High-precision numbers that do not fit an integer type are stored as floating-point numbers and may lose precision. Ill-formed input is rejected with a parse error.

Duplicate object keys

If an object contains the same key more than once, the last value is kept (the UBJSON specification does not address duplicate keys).

Type marker of optimized containers

The type marker after $ must be one of Z, N, T, F, i, U, I, l, L, d, D, H, C, S, [, or {. It is checked even if the count is 0; any other marker raises parse_error.112. A counted object typed N ({$N#i1 ...) is not supported.

Ill-formed UTF-8 in string values and object keys

UBJSON's required string encoding is UTF-8, but checking it on read is opt-in: with the error_handler parameter left at keep (the default), from_ubjson() accepts a string value or object key whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 and hands them back unchanged. Passing error_handler_t::strict makes from_ubjson() check and throw parse_error.113 for ill-formed UTF-8, and replace/ignore sanitize the string instead of keeping it. However, dump() still requires valid UTF-8 and throws type_error.316 for a value read with the default keep handler, unless an error handler is passed that replaces or ignores the ill-formed bytes. to_ubjson()'s own error_handler parameter defaults to keep (see above), so such a value is written back unchanged.

Example: deserialize a JSON value from UBJSON 
#include <iostream>
#include <iomanip>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    // create byte vector
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> v = {0x7B, 0x69, 0x07, 0x63, 0x6F, 0x6D, 0x70, 0x61,
                                   0x63, 0x74, 0x54, 0x69, 0x06, 0x73, 0x63, 0x68,
                                   0x65, 0x6D, 0x61, 0x69, 0x00, 0x7D
                                  };

    // deserialize it with UBJSON
    json j = json::from_ubjson(v);

    // print the deserialized JSON value
    std::cout << std::setw(2) << j << '\n';
}

Output:

{
  "compact": true,
  "schema": 0
}

docs.title: Element Access
docs.text:
There are many ways elements in a JSON value can be accessed:

  • unchecked access via operator[]
  • checked access via at
  • access with default value via value
  • iterators
  • JSON pointers

Testing whether a key or index exists before accessing it is also possible, with contains or find (which returns an iterator to the value, or end() if it is not found).

How do I get a value out? Start at the top and follow the first question that applies:

flowchart TD
    A["getting a value out"] --> P{{"nested path such as /server/port?"}}
    P -->|"yes"| JP["JSON Pointer: at(ptr), value(ptr, default), contains(ptr)"]
    P -->|"no, one key or index"| T{{"only testing whether it exists?"}}
    T -->|"yes"| CF["contains() / find()"]
    T -->|"no"| M{{"may it be missing?"}}
    M -->|"yes, a fallback is fine"| V["value(key, default)"]
    M -->|"yes, and missing is an error"| AT["at(): throws out_of_range"]
    M -->|"no, it exists and its type is known"| OP["operator[] and get#lt;T#gt;()"]
    OP -.- W["non-const operator[] inserts null for a missing key"]

Decision tree for reading a value: the labels on the arrows are the answers to the questions, and the boxes name the functions to use. The dashed line marks a side effect of the non-const operator[].

docs.title: Does this key exist?
docs.text:
Use contains to test for a key; it does not modify the value and does not throw:

json j = {{"name", "Mary"}, {"address", {{"city", "Berlin"}}}};

j.contains("name");                   // true
j.contains("age");                    // false
j.contains("city");                   // false: contains() only looks at the top level
j["address"].contains("city");        // true
j.contains(json::json_pointer("/address/city"));  // true: a JSON pointer tests a nested path in one call

If the value is needed afterwards, find tests and accesses with a single lookup:

if (auto it = j.find("name"); it != j.end())
{
    std::cout << *it << '\n';
}

contains also returns true for a key whose value is null; use j.contains("k") && !j["k"].is_null() if a null should count as missing. To read a value with a fallback instead, see value.

operator[] inserts missing keys

Like std::map::operator[], the non-const operator[] adds a null value if the key is missing. Testing a key with it therefore changes the object:

json j = {{"foo", 1}};
bool absent = j["bar"].is_null();   // true, but j is now {"bar": null, "foo": 1}

Use contains/find to test, and at to access a value that must exist (it throws an out_of_range exception otherwise).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The at member function performs checked access; that is, it returns a reference to the desired value if it exists and throws a basic_json::out_of_range exception otherwise.

Example: read access

Consider the following JSON value:

{
    "name": "Mary Smith",
    "age": 42,
    "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]
}

Assume the value is parsed to a json variable j.

expression value j {"name": "Mary Smith", "age": 42, "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]} j.at("name") "Mary Smith" j.at("age") 42 j.at("hobbies") ["hiking", "reading"] j.at("hobbies").at(0) "hiking" j.at("hobbies").at(1) "reading"

The return value is a reference, so it can be used to modify the original value.

Example: write access 
j.at("name") = "John Smith";

This code produces the following JSON value:

{
    "name": "John Smith",
    "age": 42,
    "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]
}

When accessing an invalid index (i.e., an index greater than or equal to the array size) or the passed object key is non-existing, an exception is thrown.

Example: access via invalid index or missing key 
j.at("hobbies").at(3) = "cooking";

This code produces the following exception:

[json.exception.out_of_range.401] array index 3 is out of range

When extended diagnostic messages are enabled by defining JSON_DIAGNOSTICS, the exception further gives information where the key or index is missing or out of range.

[json.exception.out_of_range.401] (/hobbies) array index 3 is out of range

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Exceptions

  • at can only be used with objects (with a string argument) or with arrays (with a numeric argument). For other types, a basic_json::type_error is thrown.
  • basic_json::out_of_range exception exceptions are thrown if the provided key is not found in an object or the provided index is invalid.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In many situations, such as configuration files, missing values are not exceptional, but may be treated as if a default value was present. For this case, use value(key, default_value) which takes the key you want to access and a default value in case there is no value stored with that key. This is equivalent to Python's dict.get(key, default).

docs.title: Example
Nested values
docs.text:
To read a value deep inside a document, pass a JSON Pointer instead of a key. The default value is returned if the value at the pointer does not exist, including the case that an intermediate key is missing. There is no need to check each level with contains first.

json j = {{"server", {{"port", 8080}}}, {"list", {10, 20}}};

int port = j.value("/server/port"_json_pointer, 80);        // 8080
int timeout = j.value("/server/limits/timeout"_json_pointer, 30); // 30 (missing intermediate key)
int second = j.value("/list/1"_json_pointer, 0);            // 20 (numeric tokens index arrays)
int third = j.value("/list/5"_json_pointer, 0);             // 0 (index out of range)

bool has_port = j.contains("/server/port"_json_pointer);    // true
bool has_host = j.contains("/server/host/name"_json_pointer); // false

If the path is only available as a dotted string such as "server.port", do not build the pointer by concatenating "/" and the parts: keys containing / or ~ would be misinterpreted. Append each part as a reference token with operator/= instead. It escapes the token for you.

json::json_pointer to_pointer(const std::string& dotted)
{
    json::json_pointer ptr;
    std::istringstream in(dotted);
    for (std::string token; std::getline(in, token, '.');)
    {
        ptr /= token;
    }
    return ptr;
}

int port = j.value(to_pointer("server.port"), 80);          // 8080
int first = j.value(to_pointer("list.0"), 0);               // 10

The key "a/b" yields the pointer "/a~1b"; the dot-splitting itself is up to the caller, so keys containing . need a different separator.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Exceptions

  • With string keys, value can only be used with objects. For other types, a basic_json::type_error is thrown.
  • With JSON Pointers, value can be used with both objects and arrays. For other types (null, boolean, number, string), a basic_json::type_error is thrown.

null and mistyped members are not missing

value returns the default value only if the key is absent. If the member exists, it is converted to the type of the default value, even if it is null. For {"k": null}, the call j.value("k", 0) throws a basic_json::type_error, and so does a member of another type such as a string where a number is expected. The same holds for JSON Pointers.

To treat null like a missing value, check for it explicitly:

int n = (j.contains("k") && !j["k"].is_null()) ? j["k"].get<int>() : 0;

With C++17, get<std::optional<T>>() maps null to an empty optional. As at throws out_of_range for an absent key, use find to cover both cases:

std::optional<int> n;                        // empty if "k" is absent or null
if (const auto it = j.find("k"); it != j.end())
{
    n = it->get<std::optional<int>>();       // still throws for a non-number such as "text"
}

Return type

The value function is a template, and the return type of the function is determined by the type of the provided default value unless otherwise specified. This can have unexpected effects. In the example below, we store a 64-bit unsigned integer. We get exactly that value when using operator[]. However, when we call value and provide 0 as default value, then -1 is returned. This occurs, because 0 has type int which overflows when handling the value 18446744073709551615.

To address this issue, either provide a correctly typed default value or use the template parameter to specify the desired return type. Note that this issue occurs even when a value is stored at the provided key, and the default value is not used as the return value.

#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    json j = json::parse(R"({"uint64": 18446744073709551615})");

    std::cout << "operator[]:                " << j["uint64"] << '\n'
              << "default value (int):       " << j.value("uint64", 0) << '\n'
              << "default value (uint64_t):  " << j.value("uint64", static_cast<std::uint64_t>(0)) << '\n'
              << "explicit return value type: " << j.value<std::uint64_t>("uint64", 0) << '\n';
}

Output:

operator[]:                18446744073709551615
default value (int):       -1
default value (uint64_t):  18446744073709551615
explicit return value type: 18446744073709551615

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Elements in a JSON object and a JSON array can be accessed via operator[] similar to a std::map and a std::vector, respectively.

Example: read access

Consider the following JSON value:

{
    "name": "Mary Smith",
    "age": 42,
    "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]
}

Assume the value is parsed to a json variable j.

expression value j {"name": "Mary Smith", "age": 42, "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]} j["name"] "Mary Smith" j["age"] 42 j["hobbies"] ["hiking", "reading"] j["hobbies"][0] "hiking" j["hobbies"][1] "reading"

The return value is a reference, so it can modify the original value. In case the passed object key is non-existing, a null value is inserted which can immediately be overwritten.

Example: write access 
j["name"] = "John Smith";
j["maidenName"] = "Jones";

This code produces the following JSON value:

{
    "name": "John Smith",
    "maidenName": "Jones",
    "age": 42,
    "hobbies": ["hiking", "reading"]
}

When accessing an invalid index (i.e., an index greater than or equal to the array size), the JSON array is resized such that the passed index is the new maximal index. Intermediate values are filled with null.

Example: filling up arrays with null values 
j["hobbies"][0] = "running";
j["hobbies"][3] = "cooking";

This code produces the following JSON value:

{
    "name": "John Smith",
    "maidenName": "Jones",
    "age": 42,
    "hobbies": ["running", "reading", null, "cooking"]
}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Design rationale

The library behaves differently to std::vector and std::map:

  • std::vector::operator[] never inserts a new element.
  • std::map::operator[] is not available for const values.

The type json wraps all JSON value types. It would be impossible to remove operator[] for const objects. At the same time, inserting elements for non-const objects is really convenient as it avoids awkward insert calls. To this end, we decided to have an inserting non-const behavior for both arrays and objects.

Info

The access is unchecked. In case the passed object key does not exist or the passed array index is invalid, no exception is thrown.

Danger

  • It is undefined behavior to access a const object with a non-existing key.
  • It is undefined behavior to access a const array with an invalid index.
  • In debug mode, an assertion will fire in both cases. You can disable assertions by defining the preprocessor symbol NDEBUG or redefine the macro JSON_ASSERT(x). See the documentation on runtime assertions for more information.

Exceptions

operator[] can only be used with objects (with a string argument) or with arrays (with a numeric argument). For other types, a basic_json::type_error is thrown.

docs.title: Performance: reserving array capacity
docs.text:
There is no public reserve(count) member on basic_json for pre-allocating array capacity. If you are building a large array incrementally (e.g., via repeated push_back()) and know its final size ahead of time, you can reserve capacity via get_ref() to access the underlying array_t directly:

json j = json::array();
j.get_ref<json::array_t&>().reserve(1000);
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
    j.push_back(i);
}

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
This library can create a JSON value from a wide range of inputs. This page gives an overview of the available parsing functions and how they behave; the linked pages go into more detail.

flowchart LR
    I["JSON input"] --> P["parse()"]
    I --> S["sax_parse()"]
    I --> A["accept()"]
    P -->|"optional parser callback filters values"| D["basic_json value (DOM)"]
    S --> H["events delivered to a user SAX handler"]
    A --> V["bool: is the input valid JSON?"]

The three entry points for parsing: parse() builds a basic_json value, optionally filtered by a parser callback, sax_parse() delivers events to a SAX handler, and accept() only checks whether the input is valid.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The parse function reads a JSON value from an input. The input can be

  • a string (std::string, C string, or string literal),
  • a wide string (std::u16string, std::u32string, or std::wstring, or a wide string literal),
  • a std::istream (e.g., an std::ifstream reading from a file),
  • a FILE* pointer,
  • a pair of iterators over a contiguous range (e.g., a std::vector<std::uint8_t>), or
  • a contiguous container.
// parse from a string
json j = json::parse(R"({"happy": true, "pi": 3.141})");

// parse from a file
std::ifstream f("example.json");
json data = json::parse(f);

The input must be encoded in UTF-8; other encodings are not supported. The exception is wide-character input, which is read as UTF-16 or UTF-32 — depending on the character type — and converted to UTF-8; see the parse page for an example. A single input may contain only one JSON value. Inputs consisting of multiple values separated by newlines are handled by the JSON Lines format; input that arrives in chunks or contains several values is covered in Large, streamed, and partial input.

By default, the library rejects comments and trailing commas. Both can be enabled with parameters of the parse function — see comments and trailing commas.

basic_json_document::parse accepts the same inputs with the same options, but keeps the result in a document rather than in a basic_json value; see Documents and views below.

docs.title: Strictness and trailing data
docs.text:
parse reads a single JSON value and requires the whole input to be consumed: any non-whitespace data after the value is reported as a parse error. Use it when you want to guarantee that an input is exactly one complete JSON document.

operator>> follows relaxed std::istream semantics instead: it parses one JSON value and leaves the stream positioned right after it, without requiring the rest of the stream to be consumed. This is what makes it possible to read several concatenated values from the same stream, but it also means that "a valid document followed by trailing bytes" is accepted rather than rejected. If you are validating conformance, or need to reject any input that is not exactly one JSON document, prefer parse.

When using operator>> to read several concatenated values this way, a value that is a number must be followed by whitespace, because operator>> consumes the character that terminates a number, unless JSON_PRECISE_STREAM_POSITION is defined to 1 — see the operator>> notes for details and examples.

docs.title: Input sources and performance
docs.text:
All inputs produce the same values and the same exceptions, but they are read in different ways, which makes some of them faster than others:

input how it is read strings, string views, string literals, contiguous containers, pointer or iterator ranges over contiguous memory the whole input is scanned in bulk: runs of string characters, numbers, and indentation are recognized several bytes at a time std::istream (std::ifstream, std::istringstream, ...) the characters the stream buffer holds are scanned in bulk like a string; the stream buffer is asked for more when they are used up FILE* one character at a time, with the file locked once for the whole parse other iterator ranges (e.g., std::list<char>, std::istreambuf_iterator<char>), wide strings one character at a time

Parsing a file from a std::ifstream is therefore only about 10 to 20 % slower than reading the whole file into a std::string first and parsing that, and it needs no memory for a copy of the file. The stream is never read ahead: after parsing, it is positioned exactly as if every character had been read one at a time, so operator>> can still read several values from one stream (see also JSON Lines).

Two macros switch these optimizations off without changing any result: JSON_DISABLE_STREAM_BULK_SCAN for stream buffers that do not follow the usual std::streambuf contract, and JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO for programs in which another thread must use the same FILE object while it is parsed.

Where the target has them, strings are scanned with vector instructions: SSE2 on x86-64 (and SSSE3 for UTF-8 text, when the CPU has it) and NEON on AArch64. JSON_NO_SIMD selects portable code instead, again without changing any result.

docs.title: SAX vs. DOM parsing
docs.text:
The library offers two parsing models, and a third, read-only alternative:

  • DOM parsing (the default): the complete input is read and stored as an in-memory basic_json value that can be traversed and modified freely. This is what parse does, and it is the right choice for most use cases.

  • SAX parsing: instead of building a value, the parser reports events (such as "a string was read" or "an object started") to a handler that you implement. This avoids building the full value in memory and is useful for very large inputs or when you only need to extract parts of the input. See the SAX interface for details and sax_parse for the API.

  • Document and views (<nlohmann/json_view.hpp>, added in version 3.13.0 unreleased): json_document::parse reads the same JSON grammar but builds a flat, read-only index of the values instead of a basic_json tree. Strings and floating-point numbers are read from the text on demand, and only the parts you materialize() become basic_json values. This avoids most of the work when you need only a few values from a large or frequently parsed text; see Zero-copy JSON views. It is read-only, so use parse when you need to modify the value.

You can influence a DOM parse without switching to the SAX interface by passing a parser callback, which is called during parsing and can, for example, discard parts of the input.

docs.title: Documents and views
docs.text:
A third model sits between DOM and SAX: basic_json_document::parse parses the input into a document that keeps the text and a flat index of the values in it, and basic_json_view gives read-only access to the values through that index. The whole input is validated during parsing, but only integers and strings that contain escape sequences are converted right away (the strings into a buffer owned by the document). Floating-point numbers and all other strings stay in the source text and are only converted when they are read, which is faster and uses less memory than building a tree of basic_json values when only parts of the document are needed. A document can also be modified in place, and it can be saved and loaded again without parsing it.

#include <nlohmann/json_view.hpp>

json_document doc = json_document::parse(R"({"happy": true, "pi": 3.141})");
std::cout << doc.root()["happy"].get<bool>() << '\n';

See Zero-copy JSON views for the concept and the trade-offs.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: When the input is not valid JSON, the parse function throws an exception by default. If exceptions are undesired or unavailable, the parser can instead return a discarded value, or accept can be used to only check whether an input is valid JSON. See parsing and exceptions for the available options.

docs.title: JSON Lines
docs.text:
The JSON Lines format is a text format of newline-delimited JSON. In particular:

  1. The input must be UTF-8 encoded.
  2. Every line must be a valid JSON value.
  3. The line separator must be \n. As \r is silently ignored, \r\n is also supported.
  4. The final character may be \n, but is not required to be one.

JSON Text example

{"name": "Gilbert", "wins": [["straight", "7♣"], ["one pair", "10♥"]]}
{"name": "Alexa", "wins": [["two pair", "4♠"], ["two pair", "9♠"]]}
{"name": "May", "wins": []}
{"name": "Deloise", "wins": [["three of a kind", "5♣"]]}

JSON Lines input with more than one value is treated as invalid JSON by the parse or accept functions. To process it line by line, functions like std::getline can be used:

Example: Parse JSON Text input line by line

The example below demonstrates how JSON Lines can be processed.

#include <sstream>
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    // JSON Lines (see https://jsonlines.org)
    std::stringstream input;
    input << R"({"name": "Gilbert", "wins": [["straight", "7♣"], ["one pair", "10♥"]]}
{"name": "Alexa", "wins": [["two pair", "4♠"], ["two pair", "9♠"]]}
{"name": "May", "wins": []}
{"name": "Deloise", "wins": [["three of a kind", "5♣"]]}
)";

    std::string line;
    while (std::getline(input, line))
    {
        std::cout << json::parse(line) << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

{"name":"Gilbert","wins":[["straight","7♣"],["one pair","10♥"]]}
{"name":"Alexa","wins":[["two pair","4♠"],["two pair","9♠"]]}
{"name":"May","wins":[]}
{"name":"Deloise","wins":[["three of a kind","5♣"]]}

Note

Using operator>> like

json j;
while (input >> j)
{
    std::cout << j << std::endl;
}

with a JSON Lines input does not work, because the parser will try to parse one value after the last one and throw a parse_error.101 exception. The same happens for a stream of concatenated (non-newline-delimited) JSON values: operator>> reads them one at a time, but the loop above throws after the last value. To read either format with operator>>, check for the end of the stream before each read:

json j;
while (input >> std::ws && input.peek() != std::char_traits<char>::eof())
{
    input >> j;
    std::cout << j << std::endl;
}

A value that is a number must be followed by whitespace — see the notes of operator>> for details.

docs.title: Large, Streamed, and Partial Input
docs.text:
parse reads exactly one complete JSON value and builds it in memory. It cannot be paused and resumed, and it does not hand back a half-parsed value when the input ends early. This page shows what to do when the input does not fit that model: it arrives in pieces, it contains several values, or it is too large to hold as a json value.

flowchart TD
    A["my input is..."] --> B{"several JSON values in one stream?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C["read them one at a time"]
    A --> D{"arriving in chunks (socket, pipe)?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E["frame the messages, or buffer until complete"]
    A --> F{"too large to keep in memory?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G["discard parts with a callback, or use SAX"]
    A --> H{"only a small part is needed?"}
    H -->|"yes"| I["stop early with SAX, or read through a view"]

Questions about the input and the approach this page describes for each; an input can match more than one question.

docs.title: Several values in one stream
docs.text:
For newline-delimited input, read line by line and parse each line, as described in JSON Lines. For values that are simply concatenated, operator>> reads one value and leaves the stream positioned after it. Check for the end of the stream before each read, because a read at the end throws:

Example: read concatenated values 
#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    std::istringstream input(R"({"a":1} [2,3] 4 "s")");

    // check for the end of the stream before each read, because a read at the end throws
    json j;
    while (input >> std::ws && input.peek() != std::char_traits<char>::eof())
    {
        input >> j;
        std::cout << j << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

{"a":1}
[2,3]
4
"s"

The same works for binary formats. from_cbor and its relatives accept strict = false to stop after the first value and leave the rest of the stream untouched; tellg() then reports how many bytes the value took:

Example: read one CBOR value and find out how many bytes it used 
#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

int main()
{
    // a CBOR value followed by other data
    const std::vector<std::uint8_t> cbor = json::to_cbor(json{1, 2, 3});
    std::string data(cbor.begin(), cbor.end());
    data += "TRAILING";

    std::istringstream input(data);
    json j = json::from_cbor(input, false); // strict = false: stop after the first value

    std::cout << "value: " << j << '\n';
    std::cout << "bytes used: " << input.tellg() << '\n';

    std::string rest;
    input >> rest;
    std::cout << "remaining input: " << rest << '\n';
}

Output:

value: [1,2,3]
bytes used: 4
remaining input: TRAILING

docs.title: Input arriving in chunks
docs.text:
A socket, pipe, or HTTP body hands over data in pieces of arbitrary size, and a piece can end in the middle of a number, a string, or an object. The parser does not keep state between calls, so there are two ways to deal with this.

Frame the messages. The most robust approach is a protocol that says where a value ends: one value per line (JSON Lines), a length prefix, or a delimiter. Collect the bytes of one message and parse them when the frame is complete. Prefer this whenever you control the protocol.

Buffer until the value is complete. If the data has no framing, append every chunk to a buffer and try to parse it. A parse error at the very end of the buffer means that the input ended prematurely, while an error anywhere else is a real syntax error. The member byte of the parse_error exception is one past the buffer size in the first case:

Example: buffer chunks until the value is complete 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

std::string buffer;

// call for every chunk; returns true and sets `value` once the buffer holds one complete JSON value
bool push(const std::string& chunk, json& value)
{
    buffer += chunk;
    try
    {
        value = json::parse(buffer);
        buffer.clear();
        return true;
    }
    catch (const json::parse_error& e)
    {
        if (e.byte == buffer.size() + 1)
        {
            return false; // the input ends prematurely: wait for more data
        }
        throw; // a real syntax error
    }
}

int main()
{
    json value;
    const auto chunks = {"{\"na", "me\": \"Ma", "ry\", \"l", "ist\": [1, 2", ", 3]}"};
    for (const std::string chunk : chunks)
    {
        std::cout << "chunk " << chunk << " -> " << (push(chunk, value) ? "complete" : "incomplete") << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << value << '\n';

    // a syntax error in the middle is not mistaken for missing data
    try
    {
        push("[1, ]", value);
    }
    catch (const json::parse_error& e)
    {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

chunk {"na -> incomplete
chunk me": "Ma -> incomplete
chunk ry", "l -> incomplete
chunk ist": [1, 2 -> incomplete
chunk , 3]} -> complete
{"list":[1,2,3],"name":"Mary"}
[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 5: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal

The example feeds a document in five chunks. The first four are reported as incomplete, and a syntax error is reported as such, not as missing data.

The chunks of the example, and the bytes each attempt parses again:

Buffering chunks until the value is complete: five chunks of {"name": "Mary", "list": [1, 2, 3]} appended to a buffer. After chunks 1 to 4 the buffer has 4, 12, 19, and 30 bytes, and parsing it fails at byte 5, 13, 20, and 31: one past the end, so the input is incomplete and the program waits for more. After chunk 5 the buffer of 35 bytes parses as one complete value. For the input [1, ] of 5 bytes the error is at byte 5, before the end, so it is a real syntax error. Every attempt parses the buffer from byte 1, so 4 + 12 + 19 + 30 + 35 = 100 bytes are parsed for a 35-byte value, and the work grows quadratically. chunk buffer, parsed from byte 1 each time result chunk 1 {"na error at byte 5 = size + 1 incomplete: wait for more chunk 2 {"name": "Ma error at byte 13 = size + 1 incomplete: wait for more chunk 3 {"name": "Mary", "l error at byte 20 = size + 1 incomplete: wait for more chunk 4 {"name": "Mary", "list": [1, 2 error at byte 31 = size + 1 incomplete: wait for more chunk 5 {"name": "Mary", "list": [1, 2, 3]} parsed, size 35 complete: one value other input [1, ] error at byte 5, size 5 before the end: a real error Bytes parsed: 4 + 12 + 19 + 30 + 35 = 100 for a value of 35 bytes. Every attempt starts again at byte 1, so the total work grows quadratically with the size of the value.

Each row is one parse attempt on the growing buffer: an error at the byte after the end of the buffer means the value is incomplete, an error before the end is a real syntax error. The last line adds up the bytes parsed over all attempts.

Limits of buffering

  • The buffer must contain exactly one value. Data that belongs to the next value is a syntax error. Use framing if values follow each other without a separator.
  • A number at the end of the buffer is a complete value, even if more digits are still to come (12 may be the start of 123). Buffering cannot detect this; use framing for top-level numbers.
  • Every attempt parses the buffer from the beginning, so the total work grows quadratically with the size of the value. Limit the size of the buffer for input you do not trust (see untrusted input).

docs.title: Input too large for memory
docs.text:
The input does not have to become one huge json value. The two tools below process it piece by piece.

How the memory use develops while a large array of records is parsed (illustrative, not a measurement):

Illustrative memory use over time while a large array of records is parsed, not a measurement. Four curves. D​OM, parse(): rises steadily until the whole tree is in memory. json_document: starts at about the size of the text, which it keeps, and grows a little while its index is built. Parser callback that discards every record: stays flat at the size of one record. S​AX: stays flat and lowest, because no value is built and only what the handler keeps is in memory. memory time: records parsed illustrative, not a measurement D​OM: parse() the whole tree json_document the text plus its index callback, discard one record at a time S​AX only what the handler keeps

Memory use over the number of records parsed: parse() keeps the whole tree, json_document the text plus its index, a discarding callback one record at a time, and SAX only what the handler keeps.

docs.title: Handle and discard elements with a callback
docs.text:
A parser callback is called for every finished value. If it returns false, the value is discarded and its memory is released at once. For a file that consists of one huge array (or one huge object) of records, handle each record at depth 1 and discard it:

Example: handle and discard each record of a large array 
#include <iostream>
#include <sstream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

void handle(const json& record)
{
    std::cout << "handling " << record << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    std::istringstream file(R"([{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}, {"id": 3}])");

    json result = json::parse(file, [](int depth, json::parse_event_t event, json & record)
    {
        if (depth == 1 && event == json::parse_event_t::object_end)
        {
            handle(record);
            return false; // discard the record
        }
        return true;
    });

    std::cout << "result: " << result << '\n';
}

Output:

handling {"id":1}
handling {"id":2}
handling {"id":3}
result: []

Only one record is in memory at any time. The same recipe, with more detail, is in the parser callbacks page. To skip entire members you do not need, discard them when their key is read; see the example for parse_event_t::key.

docs.title: Extract a few values and stop with SAX
docs.text:
With the SAX interface, no value is built at all, and returning false from any handler function stops the parser. sax_parse then returns false, and the rest of the input is not read. The example finds the first id in a document without parsing the remainder:

Example: stop parsing as soon as a value is found 
#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

struct find_id : nlohmann::json_sax<json>
{
    bool next_is_id = false;
    json::number_unsigned_t id = 0;

    bool key(std::string& name) override
    {
        next_is_id = (name == "id");
        return true;
    }

    bool number_unsigned(json::number_unsigned_t value) override
    {
        if (next_is_id)
        {
            id = value;
            return false; // found: stop parsing
        }
        return true;
    }

    bool null() override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool boolean(bool /*val*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool number_integer(json::number_integer_t /*val*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool number_float(json::number_float_t /*val*/, const std::string& /*s*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool string(std::string& /*val*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool binary(json::binary_t& /*val*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool start_object(std::size_t /*elements*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool end_object() override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool start_array(std::size_t /*elements*/) override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool end_array() override
    {
        return true;
    }
    bool parse_error(std::size_t /*position*/, const std::string& /*last_token*/, const json::exception& /*ex*/) override
    {
        return false;
    }
};

int main()
{
    find_id handler;
    const bool completed = json::sax_parse(R"({"x": [1, 2, 3], "id": 42, "rest": [4, 5, 6]})", &handler);

    std::cout << std::boolalpha;
    std::cout << "parse completed: " << completed << '\n';
    std::cout << "id: " << handler.id << '\n';
}

Output:

parse completed: false
id: 42

Note that sax_parse returns false both when a handler stopped the parse and when the input is invalid, so record the reason in the handler (here: id) if you need to tell the two apart.

docs.title: Read parts of a large document with a view
docs.text: If the whole text is available and you only need to read some of it, a json_document from <nlohmann/json_view.hpp> (added in version 3.13.0 unreleased) avoids the basic_json tree altogether: it keeps the text, builds a flat index of the values, and gives read-only views of the parts you look at. Only what you materialize() becomes a basic_json value. See Zero-copy JSON views for details and for the lifetime rules.

docs.title: Parsing and Exceptions
docs.text:
When the input is not valid JSON, an exception of type parse_error is thrown. This exception contains the position in the input where the error occurred, together with a diagnostic message and the last read input token. The exceptions page contains a list of examples for parse error exceptions. In case you process untrusted input, always enclose your code with a try/catch block, like

json j;
try
{
    j = json::parse(my_input);
}
catch (json::parse_error& ex)
{
    std::cerr << "parse error at byte " << ex.byte << std::endl;
}

In case exceptions are undesired or not supported by the environment, there are different ways to proceed:

Tip

Working without exceptions also covers accessing values and converting to your own types.

docs.title: Switch off exceptions
docs.text:
The parse() function accepts a bool parameter allow_exceptions which controls whether an exception is thrown when a parse error occurs (true, default) or whether a discarded value should be returned (false).

json j = json::parse(my_input, nullptr, false);
if (j.is_discarded())
{
    std::cerr << "parse error" << std::endl;
}

Note there is no diagnostic information available in this scenario.

docs.title: Use accept() function
docs.text:
Alternatively, function accept() can be used which does not return a json value, but a bool indicating whether the input is valid JSON.

if (!json::accept(my_input))
{
    std::cerr << "parse error" << std::endl;
}

Again, there is no diagnostic information available.

docs.title: User-defined SAX interface
docs.text:
Finally, you can implement the SAX interface and decide what should happen in case of a parse error.

This function has the following interface:

bool parse_error(std::size_t position,
                 const std::string& last_token,
                 const json::exception& ex);

The return value indicates whether the parsing should continue, so the function should usually return false.

Example: report parse errors without exceptions

The example derives from the library's DOM parser and overrides parse_error to print the error instead of throwing. Note the DOM parser is an implementation detail (nlohmann::detail) and may change between releases; see Do not use the detail namespace.

#include <iostream>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using nlohmann::json;

// a DOM parser that reports parse errors instead of throwing
class sax_no_exception : public nlohmann::detail::json_sax_dom_parser<json, nlohmann::detail::string_input_adapter_type>
{
  public:
    explicit sax_no_exception(json& j)
        : nlohmann::detail::json_sax_dom_parser<json, nlohmann::detail::string_input_adapter_type>(j, false)
    {}

    bool parse_error(std::size_t position,
                     const std::string& last_token,
                     const json::exception& ex)
    {
        std::cout << "parse error at input byte " << position << "\n"
                  << ex.what() << "\n"
                  << "last read: \"" << last_token << "\""
                  << '\n';
        return false;
    }
};

int main()
{
    std::string myinput = "[1,2,3,]";

    json result;
    sax_no_exception sax(result);

    bool parse_result = json::sax_parse(myinput, &sax);
    if (!parse_result)
    {
        std::cout << "parsing unsuccessful!" << '\n';
    }

    std::cout << "parsed value: " << result << '\n';
}

Output:

parse error at input byte 8
[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 8: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal
last read: "3,]"
parsing unsuccessful!
parsed value: [1,2,3]

docs.title: Where did the error occur?
docs.text:
The message of a parse_error for JSON text contains the line and column of the error:

[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 3, column 8: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal

The exception object itself only stores the byte index of the last read character in the member byte (the first byte of the input has index 1). The same index is passed to parse_error in the SAX interface. If you need the line and column as numbers, for example to show them in an editor, compute them from the input:

Example: compute line and column of a parse error 
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

// line and column (both starting at 1) of a byte index in a text
std::pair<std::size_t, std::size_t> line_column(const std::string& input, std::size_t byte)
{
    std::size_t line = 1;
    std::size_t column = 1;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 1 < byte && i < input.size(); ++i)
    {
        if (input[i] == '\n')
        {
            ++line;
            column = 1;
        }
        else
        {
            ++column;
        }
    }
    return {line, column};
}

int main()
{
    const std::string input = "{\n  \"a\": 1,\n  \"b\": ]\n}";

    try
    {
        const json j = json::parse(input);
        std::cout << j << '\n';
    }
    catch (const json::parse_error& e)
    {
        const auto position = line_column(input, e.byte);
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';
        std::cout << "byte " << e.byte << " = line " << position.first << ", column " << position.second << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 3, column 8: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal
byte 20 = line 3, column 8

Columns count bytes, so a line with multi-byte UTF-8 characters before the error may differ from the column your editor shows.

docs.title: Where is the value that caused a later error?
docs.text:
A parse_error is raised while the text is read. Many mistakes show up later: the text is valid JSON, but a value has the wrong type when you convert it (type_error.302), or a key is missing (out_of_range.403). The exception then says what is wrong, but not where in the input the value was. Define JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS before including the library to add the byte range of the offending value to such messages (since version 3.12.0), and to query the range of any value with start_pos() and end_pos():

Example: locate a value with diagnostic positions 
#define JSON_DIAGNOSTIC_POSITIONS 1
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>

using json = nlohmann::json;

// line and column (both starting at 1) of a byte index in a text
std::pair<std::size_t, std::size_t> line_column(const std::string& input, std::size_t byte)
{
    std::size_t line = 1;
    std::size_t column = 1;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 1 < byte && i < input.size(); ++i)
    {
        if (input[i] == '\n')
        {
            ++line;
            column = 1;
        }
        else
        {
            ++column;
        }
    }
    return {line, column};
}

int main()
{
    const std::string input = "{\n  \"name\": \"Mary\",\n  \"age\": \"forty-two\"\n}";
    const json j = json::parse(input); // the input is valid JSON ...

    try
    {
        const int age = j["age"]; // ... but the value has the wrong type
        std::cout << age << '\n';
    }
    catch (const json::exception& e)
    {
        std::cout << e.what() << '\n';

        // start_pos() is a 0-based index into the input; the helper expects a 1-based byte index
        const auto position = line_column(input, j["age"].start_pos() + 1);
        std::cout << "the value starts at line " << position.first << ", column " << position.second << '\n';
    }
}

Output:

[json.exception.type_error.302] (bytes 29-40) type must be number, but is string
the value starts at line 3, column 10

Positions are only available for values created by parse, they are not updated when a value is changed, and the macro makes every value 16 bytes larger on 64-bit platforms, so use it where the cost is acceptable, for example for configuration files. Note that start_pos() is a 0-based index into the input, whereas byte of a parse_error starts at 1.

For binary formats such as CBOR, there are no lines; byte is the position in the byte sequence. To find out how many bytes a successfully parsed value used, see Several values in one stream.
